findings.title: Session tokens are stored raw in the database: sessions.id IS the cookie value, unlike every other token in the codebase
findings.category: secret stored in plaintext at rest
findings.description: createSession generates 32 CSPRNG bytes (lib/auth/auth.ts:32-34), inserts them verbatim as the primary key at line 57 (`INSERT INTO sessions (id, ...) VALUES ($1, ...)`), and sets that same string as the cookie value at line 63. getSession looks it up with `WHERE s.id = $1` on the raw cookie (line 93). The file's own hashSessionId comment (lines 379-390) states the situation plainly: 'The `id` column is not a surrogate key: it is the literal bearer token stored in the httpOnly session cookie'. Every other bearer secret in this codebase is hashed before storage precisely so a database read cannot be replayed: password-reset tokens (app/api/v3/auth/forgot-password/route.ts:19,87), email-verification tokens (lib/auth/email-verification.ts:31), staff-invite tokens (app/api/v3/auth/staff-invite/[token]/route.ts:34), share tokens (AUDIT-004#secrets-01), and email 2FA codes, which even get a per-row salt (app/api/v3/auth/login/route.ts:222). API keys and TOTP seeds are at least AES-256-GCM encrypted (lib/auth/crypto.ts). Sessions are the only credential left in plaintext, and they are the highest-value one: lib/auth/impersonation.ts:103 also writes a second raw session id into the `imp_return_session` cookie.
findings.impact: Any read of the sessions table -- a leaked backup, a read replica, a blind SQL injection anywhere in 155 API routes, or a support engineer with psql -- yields directly replayable, ready-to-use session cookies for every signed-in user, including admins, for up to SESSION_TIMEOUT_DAYS (7). No further work is needed by the attacker: paste the value into a `vulnradar_session` cookie. Every other token class in the app is already immune to exactly this, so the exposure is concentrated entirely in the one place it hurts most.
findings.recommendation: Store `sha256(token)` as sessions.id and keep the raw value only in the cookie. In lib/auth/auth.ts: hash in createSession before the INSERT (line 57) and return the raw token; hash the cookie value in getSession before the SELECT (line 93) and in destroySession (line 240); hashSessionId already exists and can be reused as the digest function. The three other places that compare a raw cookie to a stored id need the same treatment: listUserSessions/findUserSessionByHash (lines 415-450, which currently hash the stored value a second time), app/api/v3/auth/sessions/route.ts:57's `s.id === currentSessionId`, and lib/auth/impersonation.ts:66-72 and :113-128. Ship it with a migration that truncates the sessions table (a forced re-login) rather than trying to convert rows in place.

findings.title: Creating an API key requires no re-authentication, so a stolen session mints a credential that outlives 'sign out everywhere'
findings.description: POST /api/v3/keys (app/api/v3/keys/route.ts:32) checks only `getSession()` and a plan limit before calling generateApiKey (lib/api/api-keys.ts:65), which returns the raw `vr_live_...` key in the response body. There is no current-password check and no rate limit on the endpoint. Every other sensitive action in this codebase does gate on re-auth: email and password change (app/api/v3/auth/update/route.ts:70-115, with its own strict `profile-reauth` login bucket), enabling TOTP (app/api/v3/auth/2fa/setup/route.ts:107-123), enabling/disabling email 2FA (app/api/v3/auth/2fa/email-setup/route.ts:258, :325), disabling 2FA (app/api/v3/auth/2fa/disable/route.ts:51), regenerating backup codes (app/api/v3/auth/2fa/backup-codes/route.ts:178), and deleting the account (app/api/v3/account/delete/route.ts:70). The API key is the one credential of the set that is not merely long-lived but independent of the session that created it: DELETE /api/v3/auth/sessions (app/api/v3/auth/sessions/route.ts:62) deletes every sessions row and does not touch api_keys, and neither does a password change (app/api/v3/auth/update/route.ts:343-350 clears sessions and device_trust only).
findings.impact: An attacker holding a session cookie for a few seconds -- an unlocked shared machine, a session lifted from a backup per auth-07, a support handoff -- creates an API key, reads it out of the JSON response, and keeps full scan/history/delete access on that account indefinitely. Every recovery action the victim knows about (sign out everywhere, change password, rotate 2FA) leaves the key working, and the only signal is one 'API key created' email that a user who did not create it is likely to dismiss. The key is also silently upgraded to the plan's real daily quota (line 93), so the cost lands on the victim.
findings.recommendation: Gate POST /api/v3/keys the same way app/api/v3/auth/update/route.ts:75-115 gates a sensitive change: require `currentPassword` in the body, verify it against `users.password_hash` behind a `keys-create:${userId}:${ip}` bucket using RATE_LIMITS.login, and skip only the password check (never the rate limit) for the null-hash OAuth-only case. Wire the field into the create-key modal in components/profile/tabs/developer/. Separately, add `UPDATE api_keys SET revoked_at = NOW() WHERE user_id = $1` to the DELETE /api/v3/auth/sessions handler, or at minimum surface active keys on that confirmation screen, so 'sign out everywhere' means what users think it means.

findings.title: GET /api/v3/admin?section=user-detail has no permission gate, so the ops role reads any user's PII, sessions and IPs without VIEW_USERS
findings.description: app/api/v3/admin/route.ts's GET gates only on requireStaff() at :81, which passes for any role at or above STAFF_ROLE_HIERARCHY.support = 10 (lib/config/client-constants.ts:39-49; ops/billing/security_analyst/content_manager are all 20). Two of its five sections then check nothing further: `section === "user-detail"` at :130 and the default stats+user-list branch at :325. The audit and active-admins sections DO gate, on hasStaffPermission(session.role, VIEW_AUDIT_LOG) at :249 and :294, which is the pattern the others are missing. user-detail returns, for any userId: email, role, plan, stripe_customer_id, subscription_status, google/github/discord identity columns, every active session row with ip_address and user_agent (:180-183), every api_keys row with prefix/limits (:168-171), webhooks, scheduled scans and internal admin notes. The ops role's grant list (lib/auth/permissions-client.ts:181-191) contains neither VIEW_USERS nor VIEW_USER_SESSIONS; billing (:145) and content_manager (:170) hold VIEW_USERS but not VIEW_USER_SESSIONS, yet all of them receive the session IP list. AUDIT-011#drift-18 flagged the matching UI cards in user-detail-panel.tsx; this is the API behind them, which a direct request reaches regardless of what the UI renders.
findings.impact: Any of the four narrow specialist staff roles - which exist precisely so an ops or content person can reach one admin tab without user data - can read every user's email, billing identifiers, linked social accounts and last-known IP addresses by calling one URL. On a ~50-user production instance that is the entire user base's PII available to a role the operator deliberately scoped away from it.
findings.recommendation: In app/api/v3/admin/route.ts, gate the user-detail branch (:130) and the default user-list branch (:325) on hasStaffPermission(session.role, STAFF_PERMISSIONS.VIEW_USERS) the same way :249 gates on VIEW_AUDIT_LOG, and drop the `activeSessions` key from the user-detail response (or the whole `sessionsRes` query) unless the caller also holds VIEW_USER_SESSIONS. Add the missing VIEW_BADGES gate to the badges branch at :281 while there.

findings.title: GET /api/v3/assets?scope=all returns host_reputation.scanned_url verbatim for every host, reintroducing the AUDIT-009 scanned-URL leak
findings.description: app/api/v3/assets/route.ts:130-174 handles `?scope=all` by selecting `host, severity_counts, findings, last_scanned_at, source_scan_id, scanned_url` from host_reputation for up to 500 rows with no owner predicate, and returns `latestUrl: r.scanned_url` at :159 to any signed-in caller. host_reputation.scanned_url is written verbatim from the scanned URL (lib/scanner/host-reputation.ts:159-186 passes `url` straight into the INSERT), query string included - normalizeHostForReputation only affects the `host` key, not this column. This is the exact exposure AUDIT-009#reputation-01 was filed and fixed for: app/api/v3/scan/reputation/route.ts:240-248 now hard-codes `scannedUrl: null` on the host-fallback branch with the comment "returning it verbatim (including its query string) to any signed-in caller who only knows the hostname would leak whatever that URL contained, e.g. a password-reset or magic-login link with a token in the query string." The assets route, added later, reads the same column with no such guard and no per-host restriction at all.
findings.impact: Any of the ~50 registered users can call one endpoint and receive the full scanned URL - path and query string - of the most recent public scan of every host in the system. A user who scans a magic-login link, a password-reset URL, a presigned S3 URL or any tokenized deep link hands that token to every other account holder. The route's own comment at :124-129 claims it "exposes nothing that isn't already public at /host/[hostname]", which is untrue: /host/[hostname] never returns scanned_url.
findings.recommendation: In app/api/v3/assets/route.ts, drop `scanned_url` from the scope=all SELECT at :139 and set `latestUrl: \`https://${r.host}\`` unconditionally at :159, matching the null-out already applied in app/api/v3/scan/reputation/route.ts:248. If a link target is needed, link to /host/[hostname] instead of the raw scanned URL.

findings.title: Support-ticket staff access is resolved from the raw session role, bypassing the ENFORCE_STAFF_2FA gate every other staff route honours
findings.description: app/api/v3/support-tickets/[id]/route.ts's GET (:77-85), POST (:194-202) and PATCH (:304-312) all call resolveTicketAccess({ ..., viewerRole: session.role }), and lib/support/ticket-access.ts:30-33 decides staff status with a bare hasStaffPermission(viewerRole, MANAGE_SUPPORT_TICKETS). That skips lib/auth/authorization.ts:35-45's passesTwoFactorEnforcement, which requirePermission/requireStaff/requireAdmin apply and which the file's own header (:15-33) describes as making "a staff-or-above account without 2FA enabled fail every requireStaff/requireAdmin check." The sibling admin inbox route app/api/v3/admin/support-tickets/route.ts does use requirePermission and is therefore gated. Concretely: with ENFORCE_STAFF_2FA on, a support/moderator/admin account with totp_enabled false is locked out of /api/v3/admin entirely (route.ts:81) but can still GET /api/v3/support-tickets/1..N, receive every ticket's full message thread plus ownerEmail and ownerName (:126-128), and POST replies that are stored with is_staff = true (:228) and emailed to the ticket owner as "Support" (:237).
findings.impact: The one hardening control that is supposed to make a staff account without 2FA harmless still leaves it able to read every customer support conversation (with the customer's email address) and to send outbound mail to customers under the product's support identity. That is exactly the blast radius the toggle exists to close, and it is the same bypass class already fixed once on the notifications and activity routes.
findings.recommendation: In app/api/v3/support-tickets/[id]/route.ts, resolve staff status through `await requirePermission(STAFF_PERMISSIONS.MANAGE_SUPPORT_TICKETS)` and pass the result into resolveTicketAccess as a boolean, instead of handing it session.role. Alternatively change lib/support/ticket-access.ts:30 to take an `isStaff: boolean` the caller computed with requirePermission, so the raw-role path stops existing.

findings.title: Staff invite emails link to /staff-invite/[token], a page that does not exist, so no staff invite can ever be accepted
findings.description: app/api/v3/admin/staff-invites/route.ts:134 builds `const inviteLink = `${APP_URL}/staff-invite/${token}`` and emails it (staffInviteEmail at :135). There is no app/staff-invite directory anywhere under app/ - the only matches for "staff-invite" are the two API route directories - so that URL 404s. The backing API pair app/api/v3/auth/staff-invite/[token]/route.ts exists and is fully implemented (GET validates a token without consuming it, POST accepts it and promotes or creates the account in one transaction), and its header at :22-30 calls itself "Public accept endpoints for a staff invite" - yet it is also absent from PUBLIC_PATHS, so even a hand-built page would be 307'd to /login for the invitee who has no account yet, which is the whole point of an invite. The admin-side UI is shipped and working: components/admin/staff/staff-list.tsx:117-127 lists pending invites and the modal creates them.
findings.impact: Every staff invite an admin sends produces an email whose only call to action is a 404. There is no fallback path: the accept endpoints have no other caller. Adding staff therefore still requires an admin to edit the target account's role by hand in the admin panel, and the invite table accumulates rows nobody can act on.
findings.recommendation: Build app/staff-invite/[token]/page.tsx: GET /api/v3/auth/staff-invite/[token] to show the invited email and role, then POST to accept (with a password field when the account does not exist yet, matching that route's POST contract). Add "/staff-invite" and "/api/v3/auth/staff-invite" to PUBLIC_PATHS in lib/config/public-paths.ts, beside the existing ROUTES.TEAMS_JOIN entry at :191 which exists for the identical "invitee has no account yet" reason.

findings.title: Bulk scan charges a daily-quota slot per URL before that URL is SSRF/access-rule validated, so blocked URLs permanently burn quota for work never done
findings.description: The bulk loop calls `const dailyQuota = await checkAndRecordRequest(authedUserId!)` at app/api/v3/scan/bulk/route.ts:637 -- an atomic check-AND-increment, so the slot is consumed at that moment -- and only afterwards calls runSingleScan at line 688. runSingleScan is where the URL is actually validated: validateScanTarget at line 104 (SSRF / private-address rejection) and checkAccessRules at line 114 (blacklist). Both return `{ success: false, error }` without ever running a scan, and there is no refund, no decrement, and no compensating call anywhere in the file. POST /api/v3/scan deliberately fixed this exact ordering and documents it at app/api/v3/scan/route.ts:196-200 ("Charging up front used to burn a scan from the daily allowance for requests that were then rejected (concurrency 429, an invalid/SSRF-blocked URL, an unverified domain) with no refund path") by moving the charge to :397, after validation and slot reservation; POST /api/v3/scan/authenticated does the same at :356. Bulk is the remaining outlier. This is a live instance of the prior 'M1 quota-charge-before-validation' backlog item (AUDIT full-audit 2026-08-25 notes).
findings.impact: A user who submits a batch containing internal, private, or blacklisted hosts (http://localhost, http://192.168.1.1, 169.254.169.254, any admin-blacklisted domain) has one daily scan deducted for each of them even though nothing was scanned. On the Free plan (25/day) a single 25-URL batch of blocked targets zeroes the account's entire day with zero scans performed, and there is no way to get it back before midnight UTC. This is self-inflicted rather than cross-tenant, but it is a support-ticket generator and it makes the used/limit numbers reported by GET /api/v3/billing describe work that never happened.
findings.recommendation: In app/api/v3/scan/bulk/route.ts, hoist runSingleScan's two gates -- validateScanTarget (currently line 104) and checkAccessRules (line 114) -- out of runSingleScan and into the loop body ahead of the checkAndRecordRequest call at line 637, pushing the rejection result and `continue`-ing without charging. Alternatively split runSingleScan into a validate step and an execute step and only call checkAndRecordRequest between them. Either shape matches the ordering POST /api/v3/scan already documents.

findings.title: An admin-gifted subscription silently overrides an active paid subscription: the paying user is dropped to the gifted plan's limits and loses every cancel / manage-billing control while still being charged
findings.category: plan resolution overrides a paid subscription
findings.description: getUserPlan resolves the effective plan as `const effectivePlan = row?.gifted_plan || row?.plan;` (lib/rate-limiting/daily-limits.ts:94) -- an active gifted_subscriptions row unconditionally wins over users.plan, with no rank comparison, so a gift of a LOWER tier replaces a higher paid tier. Every plan limit in the app flows through this (getDailyLimit :128, getUserPlanLimits at lib/billing/plan-limits.ts:96, userMeetsScheduleFrequency :182, userMeetsMinimumPlan :205). The admin gift action has no guard against an existing paid subscription: app/api/v3/admin/route.ts:1644-1700 validates only that giftPlan is a paid plan id and that giftEndDate parses, then revokes any prior gift and INSERTs the new one at :1671. GET /api/v3/billing then reports `effectivePlan = giftedSubscription ? giftedSubscription.plan : user.plan` and `subscriptionStatus: giftedSubscription ? "gifted" : user.subscription_status` (app/api/v3/billing/route.ts:247-256), and app/api/v3/auth/me/route.ts:119,175 does the same. On the client, all three subscription-management blocks in the billing tab are gated on `!billingInfo.giftedSubscription`: the subscription detail panel (components/profile/tabs/profile-billing-tab.tsx:941), the sensitive-billing reveal (:1035), and the Manage-billing / Cancel / Reactivate action group (:1415). The Stripe subscription itself is untouched and keeps billing.
findings.impact: Two concrete wrong outcomes for a real paying customer. (1) Silent downgrade: an Elite Supporter (500 scans/day) gifted Core Supporter is dropped to 100 scans/day, plus the lower apiKeys/webhooks/scheduledScans/aiTokensPerWindow/browserbaseMinutes caps, while their card is still charged the Elite price. (2) Cancellation is blocked: with giftedSubscription non-null the entire actions block at :1415 is not rendered, so the user has no Cancel, no Reactivate, and no 'Manage billing & view invoices' link to Stripe's own portal. They continue to be charged with no in-app way to stop it, which is a billing/consumer-protection exposure, not just a UI nit. Both states persist until an admin happens to run revoke_gift.
findings.recommendation: Two changes. In lib/rate-limiting/daily-limits.ts getUserPlan, pick the higher of the two rather than letting the gift win outright: compare with planRank from lib/billing/plan-limits.ts and return whichever of gifted_plan / plan ranks higher (mirror the same choice in app/api/v3/billing/route.ts:247 and app/api/v3/auth/me/route.ts:119). In components/profile/tabs/profile-billing-tab.tsx, change the three `!billingInfo.giftedSubscription` guards (:941, :1035, :1415) to gate on `!billingInfo.subscription` instead, so a real Stripe subscription always keeps its management controls and the gift panel at :1368 simply renders alongside it. Optionally warn in app/api/v3/admin/route.ts's gift_subscription case when the target already has an active stripe_subscription_id.

findings.title: Support-ticket shares survive team removal and are never re-validated at read time, so an ex-teammate keeps reading and replying to a private ticket forever
findings.description: Sharing a support ticket is restricted to teammates, but only at write time: POST /api/v3/support-tickets/[id]/shares checks areTeammates (lib/support/ticket-access.ts:57) before inserting the support_ticket_shares row at app/api/v3/support-tickets/[id]/shares/route.ts:157. The read path never repeats that check -- resolveTicketAccess grants canView on the bare existence of the row: `SELECT 1 FROM support_ticket_shares WHERE ticket_id = $1 AND shared_with_user_id = $2 LIMIT 1` (lib/support/ticket-access.ts:36-40), with `canView: isOwner || isStaff || isShared`. Nothing deletes those rows when the membership that justified them ends: DELETE /api/v3/teams/members runs only `DELETE FROM team_members WHERE team_id = $1 AND user_id = $2` (app/api/v3/teams/members/route.ts:418-421), the self-leave branch at :358 is the same, and DELETE /api/v3/teams runs only `DELETE FROM teams WHERE id = $1` (app/api/v3/teams/route.ts:209) relying on the teams-cascade, which reaches team_members and team_invites but not support_ticket_shares (instrumentation.ts:3460-3468 declares that table with FKs to support_tickets and users only, no team column). A repo-wide grep for support_ticket_shares confirms the only DELETE is the owner's explicit un-share at route.ts:195.
findings.impact: Owner shares a ticket with a teammate, then removes them from the team (or the team is deleted, or the person leaves). The removed account still passes canView, so it can read the full ticket thread -- which routinely carries account, billing and scan-target detail the owner considered internal -- and can post replies into it, appearing to the owner as a current teammate. The ticket list endpoint surfaces it too: app/api/v3/support-tickets/route.ts:42 unions `SELECT ticket_id FROM support_ticket_shares WHERE shared_with_user_id = $1` into the caller's own tickets, so the stale ticket keeps showing up in the ex-teammate's own support view indefinitely. There is no UI anywhere that lists 'tickets I still have access to', so neither party is likely to notice.
findings.recommendation: Re-validate at read time: in lib/support/ticket-access.ts's resolveTicketAccess, join the shares lookup against a current shared-team check (reuse areTeammates' self-join on team_members between opts.ticketOwnerId and opts.viewerId, or fold it into the same SQL with an EXISTS clause) so isShared is false the moment the teammate relationship ends. Also clean up eagerly: add `DELETE FROM support_ticket_shares WHERE ...` for the removed pairing to the member-removal paths in app/api/v3/teams/members/route.ts (both the :358 self-leave and the :418 removal) so the stale rows do not accumulate.

findings.title: Nothing limits requests per TARGET, nothing verifies ownership for an ordinary scan, and a wildcard robots.txt Disallow is deliberately ignored
findings.description: Every limiter in the codebase is keyed on the caller, never on the victim. Grepping `key: \`` across app/api shows the rate-limit keys are all `${userId}` or `${ip}` (plus two per-account keys for login/signup email); there is no `${hostname}`/`${rootDomain}` bucket anywhere, and lib/rate-limiting/ contains no target-side concept at all. Domain-ownership verification (isUrlOwnedByUser, lib/domains/scope.ts) is applied only when the request asks for active probes or a port scan (app/api/v3/scan/route.ts:310-324); an ordinary scan, crawl, bulk scan or schedule against any domain the caller does not own is permitted. checkAccessRules is an operator-maintained blacklist consulted on 5 of the scan entry points and absent from the two discover endpoints and the scheduled worker (see abuse-01, abuse-04); there is no shipped blocklist of sensitive target classes (.gov, financial, the product's own infrastructure). The crawler's robots.txt handling is deliberately partial: lib/scanner/crawl-discovery.ts:243 requires `value && value !== "*" && uaLower.includes(value.toLowerCase())`, so a site's `User-agent: *` / `Disallow: /` has no effect and only a group naming VulnRadar specifically is honoured (:207-216 documents this as intentional); `crawl-delay` is matched at :253 purely to mark that a rule line was seen and is otherwise discarded. On volume: one single-URL scan sends roughly 40-60 requests to the target (checkExposedFiles alone is ~23, per the comment at lib/scanner/async-checks.ts:2724 and :2799, plus checkGraphQLIntrospection up to 4 and the other live-fetch checks), and a crawl multiplies that by the page count (25 free, up to 250 elite).
findings.impact: VulnRadar will point itself at any third party on request, at a rate limited only by how many accounts the requester creates, and a site owner has no working way to opt out: the standard wildcard robots.txt directive is ignored by design, crawl-delay is discarded, and there is no abuse contact path enforced in-product. A coordinated set of free accounts converges on one victim with no server-side signal that anything unusual is happening, and every request originates from VulnRadar's IP, so the operator absorbs the abuse reports and the blocklisting.
findings.recommendation: Add a per-target bucket to lib/rate-limiting/ keyed on the registrable domain (extractRootDomain from lib/scanner/root-domain.ts) and check it in every scan entry point alongside the existing per-user check, so total inbound-to-one-victim volume is bounded across all accounts. Ship a default access-rules seed covering .gov/.mil and the deployment's own hostnames. Honour `User-agent: *` Disallow rules and crawl-delay in lib/scanner/crawl-discovery.ts for unverified domains, keeping the current ignore-wildcard behaviour only for a domain the caller has verified via isUrlOwnedByUser.

findings.title: The scan watchdog frees the concurrency slot without aborting the work, and clearCancel then makes the still-running scan uncancellable
findings.description: startWatchdog (lib/scanner/scan-jobs.ts:160-173) fires after SCAN_TIMEOUT_SECONDS (300, lib/config/config-values.ts:544) and calls only finalizeScanFailure(scanId, reason). finalizeScanFailure (:364-383) does a single UPDATE flipping status to 'failed' and then calls clearCancel(scanId) at :381. It never calls requestCancel(scanId), so the AbortController handed to the running job by getCancelSignal is never aborted -- and clearCancel deletes that controller from the cancelControllers map (:59-60), so a later requestCancel(scanId) finds nothing to abort (:48-50) and the job becomes uncancellable. Because checkConcurrentScanLimit and reserveConcurrentScanSlot count rows `WHERE status IN ('pending','running')` (lib/rate-limiting/concurrent-scans.ts:60-63, :106-109), flipping the row to 'failed' immediately returns the slot while the outbound work continues. The work genuinely outlives the row: lib/scanner/subdomain-auto.ts:101-106 deliberately keeps discoverSubdomainsForRoot running after its 15s race so it can warm the cache, and that engine's HTTP phase alone can run ~1000 names / 25 concurrency x up to 7s = several minutes.
findings.impact: concurrentScans stops being a capacity limit and becomes a bookkeeping limit. Against a deliberately slow target, a user's scans time out at 300s, hand the slot back, and start again while the previous jobs' sockets, timers and in-memory buffers are still live -- so the number of in-flight scans in the single Node process grows past every plan's cap. The operator's only lever, cancelling a runaway scan, is destroyed by the same code path.
findings.recommendation: In lib/scanner/scan-jobs.ts, have startWatchdog's timer call requestCancel(scanId) before finalizeScanFailure so the job's AbortSignal actually fires, and move clearCancel out of finalizeScanFailure into the executeScan/executeCrawlScan `finally` block that already clears the watchdog (lib/scanner/execute-scan.ts:1121), so the controller lives as long as the work does.

findings.title: GET /api/v3/ai/context does a synchronous readFileSync of a 998 KB knowledge file on every request, with no cache and no rate limit
findings.description: readKnowledgeFile (app/api/v3/ai/context/route.ts:18-26) calls existsSync + readFileSync on every invocation with no memoisation. The `finding` branch at :284-288 reads lib/ai/checks-knowledge.md -- 998,790 bytes on disk -- and then runs `new RegExp('(#{1,3}\\s+' + escapedId + '[\\s\\S]*?)(?=^#{1,3}\\s+\\S|$)', 'im')` over the whole megabyte at :299-306. The `changelog` branch at :74 reads a 250,398-byte file, `docs` at :61 reads 99,069 bytes, `checks` at :85-88 reads 71,804 (falling back to the 998 KB file when the index is missing). The route is in the set of 111 API routes with no checkRateLimit call at all: its only gate is getSession() at :29. Node's readFileSync blocks the event loop for the whole read, and this deployment is one persistent Node process shared by every user and every running scan (see the comment at app/api/v3/scan/route.ts:409-413).
findings.impact: Any signed-in user can loop `GET /api/v3/ai/context?cmd=finding&id=csp-missing` and force a 1 MB synchronous disk read plus a 1 MB regex scan per request, with no limiter to stop them. On a single-process deployment that stalls every other request and every in-flight scan's timers, and the same requests also push ~1 MB of response bandwidth each. cmd=changelog gives a cheaper-per-request but still uncapped 250 KB version of the same thing.
findings.recommendation: In app/api/v3/ai/context/route.ts, replace readKnowledgeFile with a module-level lazily-populated Map cache (the files are build artifacts and never change at runtime) or switch to fs/promises readFile, and add a checkRateLimit gate keyed `ai-context:${session.userId}` -- RATE_LIMITS.aiChat is the natural existing bucket since this endpoint exists only to feed that route.

findings.title: IP-keyed rate limits use the full IPv6 address, so an attacker with a routed /64 gets an unlimited number of fresh buckets
findings.description: getClientIp (lib/api/request-utils.ts:204-234) returns a full, unmasked address, and every anonymous limiter uses that string verbatim as its bucket key: `demo_scan:${ip}` (app/api/v3/demo-scan/route.ts:96), `login:${ip}` (app/api/v3/auth/login/route.ts:67), `signup:${ip}` (app/api/v3/auth/signup/route.ts:114), `forgot:${ip}` (app/api/v3/auth/forgot-password/route.ts:26), `resend-verify:${ip}` (app/api/v3/auth/resend-verification/route.ts:16), `contact:${ip}` (app/api/v3/contact/route.ts:35), `landing-contact:${ip}` (app/api/v3/landing-contact/route.ts:27), `public-scans:${ip}` (app/api/v3/public-scans/route.ts:49), and `ai-conversation:${userId ?? ip}` (app/api/v3/ai/conversations/route.ts:25). checkRateLimit (lib/rate-limiting/rate-limit.ts:106-176) treats the key as an opaque string, so 2^64 addresses in one routed /64 are 2^64 independent buckets. The codebase already owns the primitive to fix this: ipsInSameSubnet with configurable IPv4/IPv6 prefix bits (lib/api/request-utils.ts:120-152), used for session and API-key IP binding (lib/auth/auth.ts:160-161, lib/api/api-keys.ts:222-223).
findings.impact: Any VPS with a routed /64 or /48 -- the default allocation from essentially every hosting provider -- reduces the login limiter (5 per 15 minutes, lib/config/config-values.ts:457-458), the signup limiter (3/hour), the demo-scan limiter (5 per 12 hours, :1029-1030), and both contact-form limiters to no limit at all: rotate the source address per request. That restores unmetered anonymous scanning through /api/v3/demo-scan, unmetered signup and password-reset email sending, and online password guessing at whatever rate the account-side `login-fail:${user.id}` counter permits.
findings.recommendation: Add a `rateLimitIpKey()` helper next to getClientIp in lib/api/request-utils.ts that masks IPv6 to a /64 (and optionally IPv4 to /24) using the existing ipv6ToBigInt/ipv4ToInt masking, with the prefix widths coming from new registry settings alongside SESSION_IP_BINDING_IPV6_PREFIX. Use it for the nine bucket keys listed above; leave getClientIp itself unchanged since audit logs and session binding want the exact address.

findings.title: Report export has no rate limiter on the session path and builds the PDF synchronously over an uncapped findings array
findings.description: GET /api/v3/history/[id]/report?format=pdf reaches `Buffer.from(generatePdfReport(result))` at app/api/v3/history/[id]/report/route.ts:200. generatePdfReport (lib/reports/pdf-report.ts:11) is a synchronous pure-JS PDF builder that iterates every finding with nested word-wrap loops (:321 `for (let i = 0; i < result.findings.length; i++)`, :380-386 per code example and per code line) and applies no cap to result.findings.length. The API-key branch of the route charges checkApiKeyRateLimit at :98-101, but the session-cookie branch starting at :111 has no limiter of any kind -- the file contains no import of lib/rate-limiting/rate-limit. Before the PDF is built, the handler also loads the full findings JSONB and runs attachRemediation over it (:150-156). The same route serves format=compliance and format=md through the same unlimited synchronous path.
findings.impact: A signed-in user can loop the export of their own largest scan (a 250-page elite crawl merges findings across every page) and pin the single Node process's event loop in synchronous PDF construction, stalling every other user's requests and every in-flight scan's progress writes. There is no cost to the attacker and no server-side signal beyond CPU.
findings.recommendation: Add `checkRateLimit({ key: \`report-export:${authedUserId}\`, ...RATE_LIMITS.api })` to the session branch of app/api/v3/history/[id]/report/route.ts, and cap the findings passed into generatePdfReport (e.g. the first N by severity, with a footer noting the truncation) so a single export cannot be made arbitrarily expensive.

findings.title: Bulk scan and authenticated scan never take a concurrency slot, so the per-plan concurrentScans cap does not apply to them
findings.description: Grepping checkConcurrentScanLimit / reserveConcurrentScanSlot across the repo returns hits only in app/api/v3/scan/route.ts (:223, :363) and app/api/v3/scan/crawl/route.ts (:191, :435). app/api/v3/scan/bulk/route.ts and app/api/v3/scan/authenticated/route.ts call neither. Bulk compounds this: its INSERT at :278-279 writes the completed row in one statement with no 'pending'/'running' phase (the comment at :325 says so explicitly), so a bulk scan is invisible to the counting query in lib/rate-limiting/concurrent-scans.ts:60-63 even while it is running. Bulk is bounded only by RATE_LIMITS.bulkScan (CONFIG_RATE_LIMIT_BULK_SCAN_REQUESTS = 10 per hour, lib/config/config-values.ts:472-473) and runs its URL list inline and sequentially inside the request; ten concurrent bulk requests therefore run ten scan chains at once for a free user whose concurrentScans is 1 (lib/billing/catalog.ts:127). scan/authenticated is bounded by RATE_LIMITS.scan (100/hour) and its own daily-quota charge at :356.
findings.impact: The concurrency cap that lib/rate-limiting/concurrent-scans.ts describes as the process's real capacity limit is enforced on two of the four scan entry points. A single free user can hold ten simultaneous inline bulk scan chains, each doing full outbound check batteries, against a nominal cap of one -- and the tracking table shows zero running scans the whole time, so an operator watching concurrency has no visibility into the load.
findings.recommendation: Wrap the per-URL work in app/api/v3/scan/bulk/route.ts and the scan in app/api/v3/scan/authenticated/route.ts in reserveConcurrentScanSlot the way app/api/v3/scan/route.ts:363 does, or -- since bulk deliberately writes terminal rows -- add a lightweight per-user in-flight counter (an advisory-lock-guarded row, mirroring reserveConcurrentScanSlot) that both routes acquire and release, so all four entry points share one capacity budget.

findings.title: HTTPS targets are validated by DNS lookup and then re-resolved by undici at connect time, leaving the DNS-rebinding window the guard exists to close
findings.description: validateScanTarget (lib/scanner/safe-fetch.ts:430-494) calls `lookup(hostname, {all:true})` and rejects the target if any returned address is private, then hands back `resolvedIp = addresses[0].address`. safeFetch pins that IP into the request URL only when the scheme is NOT https/wss (lib/scanner/safe-fetch.ts:601-620). For HTTPS, the `else if (isSecureProtocol && safety.resolvedIp)` branch at lib/scanner/safe-fetch.ts:621-624 does nothing but set a Host header; the URL keeps the hostname, so undici calls `dns.lookup` again at connect time. Node has no process-level DNS cache, so an attacker serving a TTL-0 A record from their own authoritative nameserver returns a public IP to validateScanTarget's query and 127.0.0.1 / 169.254.169.254 / an RFC1918 address to undici's query. This is deterministic, not a race. The same limitation is repeated verbatim in applyPinnedTarget (lib/scanner/async-checks.ts:2747-2759, `if (parsed.protocol !== "http:") return {url, init}`) and in pinToResolvedIp (lib/scanner/safe-fetch.ts:285), so every HTTPS probe in the scanner shares it. Both places document it as accepted ("for HTTPS the protection is the DNS re-resolution happening immediately before the request"), which is not a protection at all. Note that the TLS-specific checks got this right: lib/scanner/checks/tls.ts:261-267 and lib/scanner/async-checks.ts:2268-2278 both `tls.connect({host: safeIp, servername: hostname})`, pinning the IP while keeping SNI, which is exactly the pattern the fetch layer is missing.
findings.impact: An attacker who controls a nameserver can make every HTTPS request the scanner issues land on an internal address of their choosing. Certificate validation stops them reading a response body (the cert will not match their hostname), but the TCP connect and TLS ClientHello still happen, and the difference between an immediate RST, a TLS alert, and a full timeout is a working blind port/service scanner for the network VulnRadar runs in, driven from an unauthenticated /api/v3/demo-scan request. It also means the entire private-IP block list is advisory on the HTTPS path, so any future change that relaxes cert checking (the scanner already uses rejectUnauthorized:false elsewhere) turns this into a full read primitive.
findings.recommendation: Pin the connect address without breaking SNI. In lib/scanner/safe-fetch.ts, build a per-request undici `Agent` whose `connect.lookup` returns the already-validated `safety.resolvedIp` (`new Agent({ connect: { lookup: (host, opts, cb) => cb(null, [{address: resolvedIp, family: isIP(resolvedIp)}]) } })`) and pass it as `dispatcher` in the fetch init, for https and http alike. That preserves the hostname for SNI and certificate validation while guaranteeing the socket goes to the address that was checked. Then delete the http-only branch at :601-624, apply the same dispatcher in applyPinnedTarget (lib/scanner/async-checks.ts:2747) and pinToResolvedIp (lib/scanner/safe-fetch.ts:273), and drop the "HTTPS relies on the immediate re-resolution" comments they all copy.

findings.title: The private-IPv4 block list omits 100.64.0.0/10, so Alibaba Cloud's metadata endpoint 100.100.100.200 and all CGNAT/pod-network space is reachable, along with 198.18/15 and 192.0.0.0/24
findings.description:
PRIVATE_IPV4_PATTERNS (lib/scanner/safe-fetch.ts:62-71) is the single source of truth for IPv4 filtering: isPrivateIP (:111-132) tests it directly for v4, extracts the embedded v4 out of IPv4-mapped/NAT64 IPv6 and tests it again (:123-127), and validateScanTarget (:441, :462) and port-scan's resolveSafePublicIp (lib/scanner/port-scan.ts:281-296) both delegate to it. The list is:

  /^127\./, /^10\./, /^172\.(1[6-9]|2[0-9]|3[0-1])\./, /^192\.168\./,
  /^169\.254\./, /^0\./, /^2(2[4-9]|3[0-9])\./, /^(24[0-9]|25[0-5])\./

Missing, verifiable by inspection against those eight regexes:
- 100.64.0.0/10 (RFC 6598 shared address space). `100.100.100.200`, Alibaba Cloud's instance metadata endpoint, the direct analogue of 169.254.169.254 which IS blocked on line 67, matches none of them. Neither do Alibaba's 100.100.2.136/100.100.2.138 internal DNS resolvers. The same /10 is what AWS EKS and GKE hand to pods and what carrier-grade NAT uses, so on those platforms it is live internal space.
- 198.18.0.0/15 (RFC 2544 benchmarking), routed internally on plenty of networks.
- 192.0.0.0/24 (IETF protocol assignments).
- The TEST-NET blocks 192.0.2.0/24, 198.51.100.0/24, 203.0.113.0/24.

Because isPrivateIP is also what the IPv4-mapped-IPv6 path feeds (lib/scanner/safe-fetch.ts:125), `http://[::ffff:100.100.100.200]/` is unblocked for the same reason, and so is `http://[64:ff9b::100.100.100.200]/`. Encoding variants are not a separate hole: the hostname `1684366792` (decimal for 100.100.100.200) is rejected earlier by assertSafePublicHttpUrl's `hostname.includes(".")` requirement (:529), and dotted octal/hex forms go through getaddrinfo, which normalises them before isPrivateIP sees them, but they normalise to 100.100.100.200, which is then allowed.
findings.impact: On any Alibaba Cloud deployment (VulnRadar is self-hostable and advertises exactly that), scanning `http://100.100.100.200/latest/meta-data/ram/security-credentials/` returns the instance's temporary RAM credentials in the scan result body, an unauthenticated full compromise of the host role via /api/v3/demo-scan. On AWS EKS or GKE the same /10 reaches sibling pods and node-local services. Even on a deployment where none of this is routable it is a hole in a control the rest of the product leans on: port-scan.ts, banner.ts, tls.ts and every probe in async-checks.ts all defer to isPrivateIP for their internal-range gate.
findings.recommendation: Add to PRIVATE_IPV4_PATTERNS in lib/scanner/safe-fetch.ts:62: `/^100\.(6[4-9]|[7-9][0-9]|1[01][0-9]|12[0-7])\./` (100.64.0.0/10), `/^198\.1[89]\./` (198.18.0.0/15), `/^192\.0\.0\./`, and the three TEST-NET blocks. Better still, replace the regex list with numeric CIDR containment (parse to a uint32 once and test against a table of [network, prefixLen] pairs) so a range can be stated as a CIDR and reviewed against IANA's special-purpose registry instead of being hand-encoded as a prefix regex; that also removes the class of bug in ssrf-05. Add a test to tests/lib/scanner/safe-fetch.test.ts asserting isPrivateIP("100.100.100.200") is true.

findings.title: The authenticated-scan endpoint will POST caller-supplied credentials to any public host, so it works as a credential-validation proxy against sites the caller does not own
findings.description:
POST /api/v3/scan/authenticated accepts a target `url` plus an `auth` object carrying a username and password (app/api/v3/scan/authenticated/route.ts:298-303) and hands both to establishScanSession at :334. That walks to lib/scanner/auth/browser-login.ts:456-489, which builds `username=<caller value>&password=<caller value>` plus the target's own hidden fields and POSTs it to the discovered form action via safeFetch with `Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded`, `Referer`, `Origin` and an `X-CSRF-Token` scraped from the page. The only host restriction is `allowedHostnames: [hostnameOf(origin)]`: the caller's own chosen origin.

The domain-ownership gate at app/api/v3/scan/authenticated/route.ts:312-330 fires only when `requestsActiveProbing(scanners)` is true. A plain authenticated scan of a domain the caller has never verified is explicitly allowed. The outcome is reported back distinguishably: lib/scanner/auth/browser-login.ts:496-498 returns "The target rejected the login request with 401", :505-509 returns "The login did not set or change any cookie", :511-515 returns "still showed a login form", and success returns a completed scan: the route surfaces the reason verbatim at app/api/v3/scan/authenticated/route.ts:341-346. That is a clean three-way oracle for whether a credential pair is valid on a third-party site.

The only limits are checkGlobalRateLimit on `scan-authenticated:<userId>` (:200-207) and the per-account daily scan quota (:189, :208-215). Signup is free and open, so both scale with the number of accounts an attacker creates.
findings.impact: VulnRadar's server IP becomes the origin of credential-stuffing attempts against arbitrary third-party login forms, with a built-in success oracle and CSRF-token handling already done for the attacker. The victim site's logs, lockouts and abuse reports point at VulnRadar, which for a service with a public reputation and a shared egress IP means blocklisting and abuse complaints. It also puts the operator in the position of having proxied unauthorised authentication attempts.
findings.recommendation: Apply the same ownership gate to the credential-submitting path that active-probes already has. In app/api/v3/scan/authenticated/route.ts, move the `isUrlOwnedByUser(url, authedUserId)` check at :312-330 out of the `requestsActiveProbing(scanners)` condition and require it whenever `parsed.data.auth` carries a username/password (form or basic auth); a cookie-only session (`auth.cookies`, lib/scanner/auth/login.ts:86) is the caller supplying their own already-established session and can stay ungated. Keep a per-target-host failure counter so repeated 401s against one host stop the feature for that account regardless of quota.

findings.title: Twenty docs pages are client components purely to drive a TOC scroll-spy, serializing 12,492 lines / 518 KB of static prose into the browser bundle
findings.description: Every page under app/docs/ carries "use client" (20 files, 12,492 lines, 517,607 bytes of source measured directly). The only client-side behaviour in almost all of them is two effects: one registering a static tocItems array with the docs context (app/docs/setup/page.tsx:44-47) and one wiring an IntersectionObserver scroll-spy (app/docs/setup/page.tsx:49-67). Everything else in the file is static JSX prose. app/docs/architecture/page.tsx:41, app/docs/triage/page.tsx:156, app/docs/api/page.tsx:1026 and the rest are byte-identical copies of the same two effects. The context that consumes them, components/docs/docs-shell.tsx, is already a client component, so the sidebar and TOC would keep working if the page bodies were server components. app/docs/config/page.tsx compounds it: at line 14 it imports SETTINGS_REGISTRY from lib/config/registry.ts (3,199 lines) into a client component just to render a static settings table, which is why static/chunks/6027-6257bc191d11b0fb.js (72 KB raw / 18 KB gzipped, containing setting keys, defaults and descriptions) ships to the browser on /docs/config. Measured route totals from the committed build, layout chunks included: /docs/config/page 931 KB raw JS, /docs/api/page 862 KB, /docs/setup/page 858 KB (258 KB gzipped).
findings.impact: Pages that are pure documentation, and are the pages most worth ranking (docs-shell.tsx's own comment says so), pay full client-component cost: every paragraph is serialized twice, once as HTML and again as React element JS. React hydrates thousands of static nodes on pages where nothing is interactive, and /docs/config additionally ships the whole admin settings registry to anonymous readers.
findings.recommendation: Extract the two effects into one small client leaf, e.g. `components/docs/docs-toc-spy.tsx` exporting `<DocsTocSpy items={tocItems} />` that does the setTocItems registration and the IntersectionObserver, then delete "use client" from all 20 app/docs/*/page.tsx files and render `<DocsTocSpy items={tocItems} />` at the top of each. For app/docs/config/page.tsx that also moves the SETTINGS_REGISTRY import (line 14) back to the server, removing chunk 6027 from the route.

findings.title: /host/[hostname] eagerly bundles recharts (378 KB raw / 112 KB gzipped, 25% of the route) for an optional chart that renders nothing on hosts with fewer than two public scans
findings.description: app/host/[hostname]/page.tsx:25 statically imports DangerScoreTrend, which imports recharts directly (components/host/danger-score-trend.tsx:5) and via components/ui/chart.tsx:4 (`import * as RechartsPrimitive from "recharts"`). That pulls static/chunks/1249-fe404c5fa21ca482.js, 378 KB raw / 111,822 bytes gzipped, into the route's initial JS. It is the only route in the build that references that chunk. Measured over layout + page files, /host/[hostname]/page is 1,437 KB raw / 442 KB gzipped, the heaviest route in the app; recharts alone is 25% of that gzipped total. The chart it pays for is optional and below the fold: components/host/danger-score-trend.tsx:63 returns null while its own fetch is in flight or has failed, and lines 66-81 render a text-only 'not enough public scans' branch whenever points.length < 2, which is the common case for a host with one recorded public scan. The recharts barrel is also reached through a namespace import in components/ui/chart.tsx:4, which is the one import form Next's built-in experimental.optimizePackageImports entry for 'recharts' (node_modules/next/dist/server/config.js:882) cannot rewrite into deep imports.
findings.impact: Every visitor to a public host report, including the crawlers indexing them, downloads 112 KB gzipped of charting library before anything paints, and for most hosts the chart never draws a line. /host/[hostname] is the slowest-loading page in the product by a wide margin as a direct result.
findings.recommendation: In app/host/[hostname]/page.tsx replace the line 25 import with `const DangerScoreTrend = dynamic(() => import("@/components/host/danger-score-trend").then(m => m.DangerScoreTrend), { ssr: false })`. Additionally, in components/host/danger-score-trend.tsx, move the recharts-dependent render body behind the `points.length >= 2` check into its own module so a host with one scan never fetches the chart chunk at all, and change components/ui/chart.tsx:4 from `import * as RechartsPrimitive` to named imports so Next's optimizePackageImports can rewrite them.

findings.title: The host-report trend request cannot start until the host report resolves, because the chart is mounted inside the result-gated subtree
findings.description: app/host/[hostname]/page.tsx is a client component whose entire body is gated on a useEffect fetch. The effect at line 64-85 calls `fetch(API.HOST(hostname))`; the report subtree is rendered only under `{!loading && !error && result && (` at line 179; `<DangerScoreTrend hostname={...} />` is passed as the afterSummary prop at line 277, inside that gate. DangerScoreTrend then runs its own effect (components/host/danger-score-trend.tsx:43-59) calling `fetch(API.HOST_TREND(hostname))`. The two endpoints are independent -- the trend route keys only off the hostname in the URL -- so request B is serialized behind request A for no reason. And because the page is "use client" with no server-side data fetch, the first paint for a visitor or a crawler is the skeleton at line ~150 until ~442 KB gzipped of JS parses and one round trip completes.
findings.impact: Public host reports, which are indexable pages, show a skeleton until JS has downloaded, parsed, and completed a round trip, and then wait for a second serialized round trip before the trend chart can appear. LCP on the route is two sequential network hops plus a large parse, and crawlers that do not execute JS see no report content at all.
findings.recommendation: Fetch the host report on the server. Convert app/host/[hostname]/page.tsx into a server component that awaits the same query the /api/v3/host/[hostname] route runs, issue the host and trend queries with `Promise.all`, and pass both down; keep only the interactive pieces (copy button, issue selection, back button) as client leaves. If a full conversion is too large, at minimum hoist the trend fetch out of DangerScoreTrend into the page's existing effect so both requests start together.

findings.title: /changelog ships the entire 304 KB changelog dataset to the browser (259 KB chunk, 89 KB gzipped) to render four releases
findings.description: components/changelog/changelog-list.tsx is "use client" and imports CHANGELOG from lib/changelog/data at line 7. lib/changelog/data.ts is 304,458 bytes / 4,636 lines of release records. Because the importer is a client component, the whole array is serialized into the route's client chunk: .next/static/chunks/app/changelog/page-73e8592bdfbd7e4b.js is 259 KB raw / 89,359 bytes gzipped, and the route totals 1,067 KB raw / 337 KB gzipped, second only to /host. The component then renders `INITIAL_BATCH = 4` releases (line 13) and reveals four more at a time via an IntersectionObserver sentinel. The page shell around it (app/changelog/page.tsx) is already a server component, so nothing forces the data to the client.
findings.impact: Anyone opening /changelog downloads 89 KB gzipped of release history to see four entries, and the payload grows with every release appended per the project's own changelog-per-change rule. On a phone connection this is several seconds of transfer and parse before the first four entries paint.
findings.recommendation: Keep lib/changelog/data on the server: in app/changelog/page.tsx slice CHANGELOG server-side and pass the first page of releases plus a total count into ChangelogList as props, and serve later batches from a small route handler (or a server action) that the existing IntersectionObserver sentinel calls. Alternatively render the whole list server-side as static HTML and keep only the collapse/expand behaviour client-side.

findings.title: /api/v3/auth/me is fetched two to three times per page load because TosGate and nine other call sites bypass the shared SWR cache useAuth() already populates
findings.description: components/providers/auth-provider.tsx:87 already fetches API.AUTH.ME through useSWR with a 300,000 ms dedupingInterval and exposes the result via useAuth(). TosGate, which app/layout.tsx:189 wraps around every page's children, ignores that and issues its own raw `fetch(API.AUTH.ME)` at components/auth/tos-gate.tsx:28 on every route except /login, /signup and /legal (the SKIP_TOS_PATHS list at line 9). Nine further client call sites do the same raw fetch rather than reading useAuth(): app/history/page.tsx:245, app/profile/page.tsx:283, app/checkout/[productId]/page.tsx:55, app/checkout/credits/page.tsx:34, app/checkout/browser-credits/page.tsx:35, app/checkout/github-credits/page.tsx:36, components/contact/contact-form.tsx:60 and components/shared/onboarding-tour.tsx:84. On /history that means three concurrent /api/v3/auth/me requests on a single page load (AuthProvider's SWR, TosGate's, and the page's own at line 245, which only wants `d.userId` -- a field useAuth() already returns).
findings.impact: Every authenticated page view costs two to three session lookups instead of one. With ~50 registered users this is not a capacity problem yet, but it triples the load on the hottest authenticated endpoint in the product for no functional gain, and it is the same endpoint whose transient failures already log users out (AUDIT-011 prof-03, team-03).
findings.recommendation: Have TosGate read the ToS fields off useAuth() instead of fetching: components/providers/auth-provider.tsx already types MeResponse, so add tosAcceptedAt/termsUpdatedAt to it and change components/auth/tos-gate.tsx:28 to derive status from `me`. Then replace the raw fetches in the nine listed call sites with `const { me } = useAuth()`; app/history/page.tsx:245 in particular can be deleted outright since it only reads userId.

findings.title: The notification bell and the site-notification banner both GET /api/v3/notifications/active with identical parameters on every page load, then each filter the same payload client-side
findings.description: components/shared/site-notifications.tsx:674-706 (SiteNotificationsWrapper, mounted at app/layout.tsx:188) builds `?authenticated=..&staff=..` and fetches /api/v3/notifications/active, then keeps only type banner/modal/toast. components/shared/notification-center.tsx:290-319 builds the same two params, fetches the same URL, and keeps only type bell -- and re-polls it on setInterval every clientConfig.notificationPollIntervalMs (default CONFIG_NOTIFICATION_POLL_INTERVAL_MS = 300000, lib/config/config-values.ts:1097). A second interval at components/shared/notification-center.tsx:344 polls API.NOTIFICATIONS on the same schedule. So every page load issues two identical requests for one payload, and every open tab keeps one of them cycling forever.
findings.impact: Every page view in the app doubles the request count and the database work for site notifications, including anonymous visitors on the public marketing pages (the wrapper runs regardless of sign-in state). The duplication is invisible in normal use, which is exactly why it will not be noticed as traffic grows.
findings.recommendation: Fetch /api/v3/notifications/active once and share it. Move the fetch into a small SWR hook (e.g. lib/hooks/use-active-notifications.ts) keyed on the `authenticated`/`staff` params, have both SiteNotificationsWrapper (components/shared/site-notifications.tsx:687) and NotificationCenter (components/shared/notification-center.tsx:297) consume it, and keep the type filtering where it is. SWR's dedupingInterval then collapses the two calls into one and the existing 5-minute refresh becomes a single revalidation.

findings.title: pollScanStatus has no abort path, so navigating away from the dashboard mid-crawl keeps polling every 2 seconds for up to 16 minutes
findings.description: app/dashboard/page.tsx:128-164 defines `pollScanStatus` as a bare async while-loop: `while (Date.now() - startedAt < maxWaitMs)` fetches API.SCAN_STATUS(scanId), then `await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, pollIntervalMs))`. It accepts no AbortSignal and checks no cancellation flag. It is awaited from runScan at line 597 with maxWaitMs = SCAN_MAX_WAIT_MS (6 min, line 87) or CRAWL_MAX_WAIT_MS (16 min, line 88) and pollIntervalMs from useClientConfig, defaulting to CONFIG_SCAN_STATUS_POLL_INTERVAL_MS = 2000 (lib/config/config-values.ts:555). runScan is a useCallback fired from an event handler, and nothing in the component's effects (lines 271, 302, 707, 784) tears the loop down. In App Router client navigation the JS context survives route changes, so a user who starts a deep crawl and clicks through to /history leaves the loop running: 16 minutes at 2 s is up to 480 requests to a status endpoint whose result no mounted component can use. cancelledRef (line 203) only guards the UI reset after the loop settles; the loop itself never reads it.
findings.impact: A user who starts a crawl and navigates away, or opens the dashboard in a background tab and forgets it, generates hundreds of pointless authenticated status requests. Multiplied across concurrent users this is measurable database and event-loop load on the same process that is running the scan, which the audit-011 finding scan-06 already shows has no yields to spare.
findings.recommendation: Give pollScanStatus an AbortSignal: thread an AbortController through runScan, pass `signal` to the fetch at app/dashboard/page.tsx:142, break the loop when `signal.aborted`, and abort it from a `useEffect(() => () => controller.abort(), [])` cleanup in DashboardContent plus from handleCancelScan (line 804).

findings.title: No poller anywhere in the app pauses when the tab is hidden: there is not one visibilitychange or document.hidden reference in the codebase
findings.description: Grepping visibilitychange and document.hidden across app/, components/ and lib/ returns zero matches. Every recurring timer therefore keeps firing in a backgrounded tab: components/shared/notification-center.tsx:314 and :344 (two polls of /api/v3/notifications/active and API.NOTIFICATIONS every 300,000 ms by default), app/dashboard/page.tsx:140 (scan status, 2,000 ms, up to 16 minutes), app/browser/[id]/page.tsx:327 (browser session logs at LOGS_POLL_MS) and :202 (a 1,000 ms clock tick), components/admin/features/backup-manager.tsx:106 (2,000 ms), components/admin/features/updater-manager.tsx:171 (2,000 ms), components/admin/features/queue-status-manager.tsx:65 (45,000 ms), components/scanner/subdomain-discovery.tsx:202. Browsers throttle setTimeout/setInterval in hidden tabs to roughly 1/minute after a delay, but they do not stop fetches that a still-scheduled timer issues, and the 45 s and 300 s pollers are already slower than the throttle floor so they run essentially unthrottled.
findings.impact: Users who leave the dashboard, an admin panel, or any page with the notification bell open in a background tab keep issuing authenticated, database-backed requests indefinitely. For an operator this shows up as a persistent request floor proportional to open tabs rather than to active users, and it is the kind of load that only becomes visible after the user base grows.
findings.recommendation: Add a shared hook, e.g. lib/hooks/use-visible-interval.ts, that wraps setInterval and clears/restarts on document visibilitychange, and use it at components/shared/notification-center.tsx:314 and :344, components/admin/features/queue-status-manager.tsx:65, components/admin/features/backup-manager.tsx:106 and components/admin/features/updater-manager.tsx:171. For the fast pollers that track a real job (dashboard scan status, browser session logs) keep them running but back the interval off while hidden rather than stopping outright.

findings.title: /admin eagerly imports 22 manager components into one 1,333 KB route and renders a single tab at a time
findings.description: app/admin/page.tsx is a 1,683-line client component that statically imports 22 admin panels at lines 46-60 and 91-150 (IPRulesManager, BlockedDataManager, ContentManager, SecurityAlertsManager, SystemSettingsManager, MassEmailManager, AIChatsManager, SupportInbox, UpdaterManager, BackupManager, ErrorLogsManager, EmailLogsManager, EngineFeedbackManager, QueueStatusManager, BillingOverviewManager, NotificationsManager, UserDetailPanel, AuditLog, StaffList, TeamsList and others). Each is itself large -- components/admin/users/user-detail-panel.tsx is 2,925 lines, components/admin/staff/staff-list.tsx 1,234, components/admin/notifications/notifications-manager.tsx 1,080, components/admin/features/ip-rules-manager.tsx 970. They render one at a time behind `activeTab === ...` guards (e.g. line 1182), but all 22 are in the initial bundle. Measured over layout + page files, /admin/page is 1,333 KB raw JS, the second heaviest route in the build.
findings.impact: Every admin page load downloads and parses 1.3 MB of JavaScript, of which one panel is used. Staff on slow connections wait through the whole payload before the admin shell is interactive, and each new admin panel added makes the first paint of every other tab slower.
findings.recommendation: Convert the tab panels in app/admin/page.tsx to `next/dynamic` imports with a skeleton fallback (the file already imports `dynamic` nowhere, but app/dashboard/page.tsx:5 and app/profile/page.tsx:5 establish the pattern). Start with the four largest -- UserDetailPanel, StaffList, NotificationsManager, IPRulesManager -- which alone account for over 6,200 lines.

findings.title: images.unoptimized is on and Discord sign-in avatars are stored without a ?size= parameter, so 1024px PNGs are downloaded to fill 14px circles on /public-scans
findings.description: next.config.mjs:25-27 sets `images: { unoptimized: true }`, which turns every next/image into a pass-through with no resizing and no format negotiation. lib/auth/oauth-userinfo.ts:231 builds the Discord sign-in avatar URL as `https://cdn.discordapp.com/avatars/${data.id}/${data.avatar}.png` with no size query parameter, so Discord's CDN serves the full-resolution PNG (the same file elsewhere in the codebase is requested with an explicit cap: components/profile/tabs/profile-social-tab.tsx:636 uses ?size=128 and app/api/v3/account/discord/route.ts:181 uses ?size=256). GitHub avatars at lib/auth/oauth-userinfo.ts:203 store the raw avatar_url, which githubusercontent serves at its default resolution. Those stored URLs are then rendered at thumbnail size: components/public-scans/public-scan-row.tsx:80 renders `` for every row of the public scans directory, and components/admin/shared/user-avatar.tsx:32 renders width={48} into `h-7 w-7` (28px) rows. Locally uploaded avatars are unaffected -- components/modals/image-crop-dialog.tsx:167 crops them to 256px before upload -- so this is specifically the OAuth-provider path.
findings.impact: A page of the public scans directory can pull one full-resolution provider avatar per row to render 14x14 thumbnails. A Discord PNG at default resolution is commonly a few hundred kilobytes, so a 20-row listing can transfer several megabytes of avatar data for roughly 4 KB of rendered pixels, on a page anonymous visitors and crawlers hit.
findings.recommendation: Append a size cap where the URL is built: change lib/auth/oauth-userinfo.ts:231 to `...png?size=128` (matching the connect flow at app/api/v3/account/discord/route.ts:181) and lib/auth/oauth-userinfo.ts:203 to append `&s=128` to the GitHub avatar_url. Separately, reconsider `images: { unoptimized: true }` in next.config.mjs:26 -- sharp is already pinned in the package.json overrides, so enabling the optimizer with remotePatterns for the three provider CDNs would fix the existing stored URLs too.

findings.title: The DNS branch issues roughly 90-110 lookups per scan with no memoization, including four identical MX queries and 52 DKIM probes it never short-circuits
findings.description: `checkDNSSecurity` fires 28 sub-checks in one `Promise.allSettled` (lib/scanner/async-checks.ts:2114) and none of them share a resolver cache. The same record is resolved repeatedly: `dns.resolveMx(domain)` runs four times (lines 1444 hasNullMX, 1465 checkMX, 1513 checkBackupMX, 1555 checkMXHostnameCname); `dns.resolveTxt(domain)` twice (129 checkSPF, 262 checkSPFChain); `dns.resolveSoa(domain)` twice (1603, 1649); `dns.resolveNs(domain)` twice (1083, 2035); `dns.resolveTxt('_mta-sts.' + domain)` twice (1134, 1174). Worse, `checkDKIM` probes 26 hardcoded selectors (list at lines 618-663) via `Promise.allSettled(selectors.map(probeDKIMSelector))` at line 700, and `probeDKIMSelector` does a TXT lookup (line 673) and, on failure, a CNAME lookup (line 688) -- so a domain with no DKIM, the case that produces the finding, costs 52 queries. There is no early exit once a selector hits, and `checkDKIMWeakKey` (line 775) then re-probes 10 of the same selectors.
findings.impact: One scan of one domain fires roughly 90-110 DNS queries in a burst, of which about 15 are exact duplicates. Against a rate-limiting or slow recursive resolver this is what pushes the `dns` branch into its 12s `SCANNER_ASYNC_BRANCH_TIMEOUT_MS` ceiling (lib/config/config-values.ts:615), which drops every DNS finding and downgrades the reported engine confidence. On a crawl it multiplies by the page count (see perf-03).
findings.recommendation: Add a small per-scan (or short-TTL per-host) memo in lib/scanner/async-checks.ts wrapping `dns.resolveTxt/resolveMx/resolveNs/resolveSoa/resolveCname`, keyed on (type, name), so the 28 sub-checks share one resolution per record. In `probeDKIMSelector`, race the selectors with an early exit once one is found rather than always running all 26 to completion, and have `checkDKIMWeakKey` reuse `checkDKIM`'s already-fetched TXT records instead of re-resolving.

findings.title: validateScanTarget does an uncached blocking dns.lookup on every call and is invoked 12-20 times per scan, all of it through the four-thread libuv pool
findings.category: repeated blocking resolution on a shared threadpool
findings.description: `validateScanTarget` resolves the target with `await lookup(hostname, { all: true })` (lib/scanner/safe-fetch.ts:460) and caches nothing. `safeFetch` calls it once per request (line 584) and again on every redirect hop (line 746), and it is additionally called directly from app/api/v3/scan/route.ts:276, lib/scanner/checks/tls.ts:104/247/359, lib/scanner/async-checks.ts:2251/2732/3566/3648/3755, lib/scanner/active-probes/shared.ts:160, lib/scanner/active-probes/open-redirect.ts:155, lib/scanner/subdomain-auto.ts:99 and lib/scanner/page-screenshot.ts:199. A single scan of one host therefore resolves that host 12-20 times. Unlike `dns.resolve*`, `dns.lookup` is `getaddrinfo` and runs on the libuv threadpool, which defaults to 4 threads; nothing in the repo sets `UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE` (no occurrence anywhere outside node_modules), and that same pool serves `fs` and node:crypto's async KDFs.
findings.impact: The scan pays 12-20 identical resolutions it could pay once. More importantly, concurrent scans queue on four OS threads: with a resolver that takes 100ms, eight simultaneous scans serialize their SSRF checks and also stall unrelated filesystem and crypto work in the same process. VulnRadar runs as one persistent Node process, so this is process-wide back-pressure, not per-request.
findings.recommendation: Add a short-TTL (5-15s) in-process memo in front of `validateScanTarget` in lib/scanner/safe-fetch.ts keyed on hostname, returning the cached `SafetyCheckResult`. The TTL must stay short so the DNS-rebinding protection the function exists for is preserved -- a 10s window is still far tighter than a scan's own lifetime. Separately, set `UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE` in the Dockerfile/start script to something matched to the box (16 is a common default for I/O-heavy Node services).

findings.title: GET /api/v3/auth/me issues seven queries per call, reading the same users row three times and gifted_subscriptions twice, and it runs on every page load
findings.category: redundant queries on the hottest authenticated route
findings.description: `getSession()` at app/api/v3/auth/me/route.ts:61 already runs `SELECT ... FROM sessions s JOIN users u ON s.user_id = u.id WHERE s.id = $1` (lib/auth/auth.ts:98-104). The route then runs a six-way `Promise.all` at line 79 which reads the same users row again (lines 80-88), reads `gifted_subscriptions` (lines 96-99), and calls `getUserPlanLimits(session.userId)` (line 110) which calls `getUserPlan` (lib/rate-limiting/daily-limits.ts:75) -- a third read of the users row joined against gifted_subscriptions a second time. Net: 7 queries, 6 of them concurrent out of a pool whose max is 10 (lib/config/config-values.ts:393), for data that is one users row, one badges join, and one discord row.
findings.impact: This is the endpoint `AuthProvider` calls on every page navigation, so it is the highest-frequency authenticated query in the product. Every page view costs 7 database round trips instead of 3, and two simultaneous page loads from different users take 12-14 of the 10 available pool connections, forcing everything else in the process to queue.
findings.recommendation: Have `getSession` return (or a request-scoped cache hold) the users row so lines 80-88 do not re-read it, and pass the already-fetched plan into `getUserPlanLimits` instead of letting it call `getUserPlan` again. Fold the `gifted_subscriptions` lookup into the single users query with a LEFT JOIN, exactly as `getUserPlan` already does. That takes the route from 7 queries to 3.

findings.title: The scan progress tracker writes two UPDATEs to scan_history per category, so a single scan does about 40 row rewrites of the widest table in the schema
findings.description: `createProgressTracker`'s `onProgress` hook fires an `UPDATE scan_history SET current_category = $1, categories_total = $2 WHERE id = $3` on every "start" event (lib/scanner/scan-jobs.ts:120-127) and an `UPDATE scan_history SET categories_completed = $1, categories_total = $2 ...` on every "done" event (lines 131-138). The hook is invoked twice per category by `runSyncChecks` (lib/scanner/engine.ts:166 and :203) and twice per branch by `runAsyncChecksDetailed` (lib/scanner/async-checks.ts:4642 and :4644). `categoriesTotal` is `plannedSync.length + plannedAsync.length` (app/api/v3/scan/route.ts:339), which for a default full scan is roughly 16 sync categories plus 4-5 async branches -- about 40 UPDATEs per scan. Because Postgres is MVCC, each one writes a new version of a `scan_history` row that carries the `findings`, `summary`, `response_headers` and `result_meta` JSONB columns.
findings.impact: About 40 dead tuples per scan on the largest table in the schema, plus 40 write round trips competing for the same 10-connection pool the scan's own reads use. On a crawl this is 40 x page count. It also inflates autovacuum work on the one table every list, dashboard and public page reads from.
findings.recommendation: Coalesce progress writes in lib/scanner/scan-jobs.ts:113: keep the counters in memory and flush at most once every ~500ms (or only when `current_category` actually changes) with a single UPDATE, dropping the separate start/done writes. The status poll already runs on a 2s interval (AUDIT-011 scan-03), so sub-second progress precision buys nothing.

findings.title: GET /api/v3/ai/context reads up to 998KB from disk with readFileSync on every request, uncached, and resolves the session twice
findings.category: uncached synchronous file I/O on a request path
findings.description: `readKnowledgeFile` does `existsSync` then `readFileSync(p, 'utf8')` (app/api/v3/ai/context/route.ts:20-22) with no memoization. The files it serves are lib/ai/checks-knowledge.md at 998,790 bytes, lib/ai/changelog-knowledge.md at 250,398 bytes, lib/ai/docs-knowledge.md at 99,069 bytes, lib/ai/checks-index.md at 71,804 bytes and lib/ai/legal-knowledge.md at 34,746 bytes. They are build artifacts (generated by scripts/compile-*-knowledge.mjs) and never change at runtime. The `/finding` command additionally reads the full 998KB file at line 284 and then runs a regex with a lazy `[\s\S]*?` and a lookahead across the whole string (lines 302-306). Separately, `GET` already calls `getSession()` at line 29, and the `history`, `me` and `stats` branches call it again at lines 115, 230 and 327 -- two session queries per request on those paths.
findings.impact: `readFileSync` blocks the event loop for the whole read, so every /checks or /finding slash command in the AI chat stalls the single Node process serving all users for the duration of a 1MB synchronous read plus a 1MB UTF-8 decode plus a 1MB regex scan. Nothing about these files justifies re-reading them; they are identical between every request until the next deploy.
findings.recommendation: Load each knowledge file once into a module-level `Map<string, string>` on first use in app/api/v3/ai/context/route.ts and serve from memory thereafter (the process restarts on deploy, so staleness is impossible). For `/finding`, build an id -> section index once at first load instead of regex-scanning the full document per request. Pass the already-resolved `session` from `GET` into `handleContext` instead of calling `getSession()` a second time at lines 115, 230 and 327.

findings.title: An invalid API key falls through to a full scan of the legacy key rows and a bcryptjs comparison per row, on the main thread
findings.category: unbounded work on an unauthenticated failure path
findings.description: `validateApiKey` tries the O(1) locator lookup first (lib/api/api-keys.ts:336), but when it matches nothing it does not return. It then runs `SELECT ... WHERE ak.key_locator IS NULL AND ak.key_encrypted IS NOT NULL` (line 362) and AES-decrypts every returned row, and then `SELECT ... WHERE ak.key_hash IS NOT NULL AND ak.key_locator IS NULL AND ak.key_encrypted IS NULL` (line 392) and calls `verifyKey(key, row.key_hash)` for every row in a `for` loop (line 404). `verifyKey` is `bcrypt.compare` from `bcryptjs` (lines 2 and 126) -- the pure-JavaScript implementation, which does its work on the main thread rather than the libuv pool -- against hashes generated at cost 12 (`const saltRounds = 12`, line 120). Only on a match is the locator backfilled (line 376), so a legacy key that is never used again keeps its row in the scanned set forever.
findings.impact: Every request with a wrong, revoked or stale Bearer token costs three extra queries and one main-thread bcrypt-12 comparison per un-backfilled legacy row. bcryptjs at cost 12 is on the order of 200-400ms of JavaScript CPU per comparison, so a handful of legacy rows turns each bad token into a second or more of event-loop time in a single-process deployment -- and POST /api/v3/scan reaches this before any rate limiting applies (app/api/v3/scan/route.ts:65).
findings.recommendation: In lib/api/api-keys.ts:326, return `null` immediately after the locator lookup misses unless a one-time startup check confirms un-backfilled rows still exist (`SELECT EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM api_keys WHERE key_locator IS NULL)`, cached in module scope and cleared on key creation). Run the backfill as a migration in instrumentation.ts rather than lazily on match, then delete the two fallback scans entirely.

findings.title: Nine missing indexes: four force full table scans inside the single long cleanup transaction, two make per-scan triage lookups degrade with total history
findings.description: Cross-checking every index in instrumentation.ts against the WHERE/JOIN/ORDER BY columns in app/ and lib/ leaves these gaps. (1) `rate_limits.window_start` has no index -- `UNIQUE(key, window_start)` (instrumentation.ts:842) leads on `key` -- so `DELETE FROM rate_limits WHERE window_start < NOW() - INTERVAL '1 day'` (lib/database/cleanup.ts:211) seq-scans the fastest-growing table in the schema. (2)(3)(4) The same shape on `scan_finding_feedback.created_at` (cleanup.ts:380), `user_notifications.created_at` (cleanup.ts:389) and `github_review_usage.updated_at` (cleanup.ts:401): each table's only timestamp index is a composite led by `user_id` (instrumentation.ts:1471, 1672, 2047), unusable as a timestamp-only scan key -- while admin_audit_log, email_logs, system_error_logs and api_usage all do have the plain index their identical prune uses. (5) `ai_conversations.last_message_at` has no index; the table has `idx_ai_conversations_created_at` (instrumentation.ts:1191) on the wrong column, and both real consumers use `last_message_at` (cleanup.ts:353 and app/api/v3/ai/conversations/route.ts:171-175, which also sorts by it). (6)(7) `finding_remediation(user_id, finding_url)` and `scan_finding_feedback(user_id, finding_url)`: both tables have `UNIQUE (user_id, finding_id, finding_url)` (instrumentation.ts:1516, 1467), with `finding_id` sitting between the two columns the hot queries actually filter on (lib/scanner/remediation-store.ts:41-44, lib/scanner/regression-alert.ts:47-49), so only `user_id` is usable as a key. (8) `broadcast_recipients(message_id, user_id)` -- see perf-07. (9) the public-shares partial index -- see perf-04.
findings.impact: The cleanup pass (lib/database/cleanup.ts) performs four full table scans on the largest, fastest-growing tables, all inside one transaction (see perf-22). `getRemediationMap` runs on every scan-result render and `regression-alert` after every completed scan; both currently cost O(that user's entire triage history) instead of O(findings for this URL), so a heavy user's scans get slower the more findings they have ever triaged. The admin AI-conversations page seq-scans and externally sorts a table of JSONB message arrays on every load.
