findings.recommendation: Add to the performance-index block in instrumentation.ts (around line 1587): `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_rate_limits_window_start ON rate_limits(window_start); CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_ai_conversations_last_msg ON ai_conversations(last_message_at DESC); CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_user_notifications_created ON user_notifications(created_at); CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_sff_created ON scan_finding_feedback(created_at); CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_gru_updated ON github_review_usage(updated_at); CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_finding_remediation_user_url ON finding_remediation(user_id, finding_url); CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_sff_user_url ON scan_finding_feedback(user_id, finding_url);` Keep the existing three-column UNIQUEs -- they back the `ON CONFLICT` clauses in app/api/v3/scan/remediation/route.ts:93 and app/api/v3/scan/feedback/route.ts:60. `idx_ai_conversations_created_at` has no reader and can be dropped.

findings.title: Four hot queries wrap an indexed column in a function or regex, so the index that exists for them can never be used
findings.description: (a) app/api/v3/host/[hostname]/trend/route.ts:77-82 filters `WHERE is_public = true AND status = 'completed' AND url ~* $1`, with `$1` built as `^https?://(www\.)?<host>([:/?]|$)` at line 70. `~*` is not a b-tree-indexable operator, so `idx_scan_history_url_public_completed` (instrumentation.ts:2359) degrades to a full scan applying a case-insensitive regex to every row, then a sort, and only then `LIMIT 30`. The query also selects the full `findings` JSONB for those 30 rows. This is a public unauthenticated page. (b) app/api/v3/dashboard/route.ts:75 joins on `DATE(sh.scanned_at) = days.day` (see perf-06). (c) lib/domains/scope.ts:47-53 filters `($1 = domain OR $1 LIKE '%.' || domain)` -- the LIKE pattern is built from the column with the parameter on the left, which no b-tree can serve, so `idx_domains_domain_verified` (instrumentation.ts:3189) is unusable and every scan authorization check scans all verified domains across all tenants. (d) app/api/v3/admin/blocked-data/route.ts:60-83 and its DELETE twin at :124-135 apply `LOWER(REGEXP_REPLACE(sh.url, ...))` per row over all of scan_history before the `LIMIT 100`.
findings.impact: Each of these reads the whole table where an index exists specifically to prevent that. (a) and (c) are the ones that matter operationally: (a) is on an unauthenticated route whose cost grows with total public scan volume, and (c) runs on the authorization gate for every active-probe or port-scan request.
findings.recommendation: For (a), store the normalized host at scan time (a `host` column populated from lib/scanner/root-domain.ts, indexed) and filter `WHERE host = $1` instead of regexing the URL; also stop selecting `findings` there and project only title/severity. For (b), rewrite as a range predicate. For (c), store the registrable domain and each of its parent suffixes so the lookup becomes `domain = ANY($1::text[])`, which is indexable. For (d), the same normalized `host` column removes the REGEXP_REPLACE.

findings.title: The root layout reads headers() for a CSP nonce, which forces all ~790 public SEO pages to be server-rendered per request with no static or ISR output
findings.category: no static rendering anywhere in the app
findings.description: `RootLayout` does `const nonce = (await headers()).get('x-nonce') ?? undefined` at app/layout.tsx:146. The comment above it (lines 139-145) states the consequence outright: this "forces this layout (and everything under it) into per-request dynamic rendering". app/checks/[id]/page.tsx repeats it at lines 29-31 -- `generateStaticParams` still enumerates the id space (line 34) but the pages are never actually prerendered. `getAllChecks()` returns the full check inventory (lib/seo/checks-content.ts:142), which is the ~754-page /checks tree, plus /checks/category/*, /docs, /finding-types, /host/* and the legal pages -- roughly 790 public routes, every one of which runs the full React server render on every single hit.
findings.impact: Googlebot crawling the /checks tree, or any traffic to the SEO surface the project deliberately built for discovery, costs a full server render per page view with zero cache. The same CPU is shared with the scan engine's synchronous check loop (AUDIT-011 scan-06) in one Node process, so crawler traffic directly slows scans. It also means `next build` produces no static output for content that never changes between deploys.
findings.recommendation: Move the nonce out of the layout's render. Either (a) have middleware.ts inject the nonce into the response HTML stream so the layout stays static, or (b) switch the CSP for the static content routes to a hash-based or `strict-dynamic`-with-no-nonce policy, and drop the `headers()` read from app/layout.tsx so /checks, /docs and the legal pages can be prerendered and revalidated on a long interval. Keep the nonce path for the authenticated app routes that genuinely need per-request rendering.

findings.title: POST /api/v3/scan/bulk does roughly nine sequential database round trips per URL, up to 900-1000 in one request, and takes a row lock on the API key each time
findings.description: The bulk route loops `for (let i = 0; i < urlsToScan.length; i++)` at app/api/v3/scan/bulk/route.ts:622 with every step awaited in order. Per iteration: `checkAndRecordRequest` (line 637) costs `getDailyLimit` -> `getUserPlan` plus an UPSERT and possibly a re-read (lib/rate-limiting/daily-limits.ts:309/330/361/378) = 2-3 queries; `checkApiKeyRateLimit` (line 668) runs `pool.connect` + BEGIN + `SELECT id FROM api_keys WHERE id = $1 FOR UPDATE` (lib/api/api-keys.ts:489) + a 24h `COUNT(*)` over api_usage (line 505) + an INSERT (line 514) + COMMIT + an `UPDATE api_keys SET last_used_at` (line 528) + a `SELECT used_at ... LIMIT 1` (line 543) = 7 round trips holding a row lock; `runSingleScan` (line 688) adds `checkAccessRules` (2 queries) and an `INSERT INTO scan_history`. `MAX_URLS_BULK` defaults to 100 (lib/config/config-values.ts:543).
findings.impact: A 100-URL bulk request performs on the order of 900-1000 serialized database round trips inside one HTTP handler, acquiring and releasing a `FOR UPDATE` lock on the same api_keys row 100 times, while holding pool connections throughout. Even at 2ms RTT that is two seconds of pure database latency layered on top of 100 sequential network scans.
findings.recommendation: Hoist the per-user work out of the loop in app/api/v3/scan/bulk/route.ts:622: resolve the plan and daily limit once, charge quota for the whole batch in one capped statement, and record API usage once per batch (or as a single multi-row INSERT at the end) rather than per URL. Cache the access-rules result per host for the duration of the request.

findings.title: Four routes select the full findings JSONB for an unbounded row set, including a GDPR export that buffers the entire admin audit log into memory twice
findings.description: (a) app/api/v3/shares/route.ts:15-30 selects `summary, findings` for every share a user owns with no LIMIT, then JSON.parses each blob in JS at lines 32-36 -- and the only derived value is `findingsCount: findings.length` (line 50), which the `findings_count` column already stores. (b) app/api/v3/admin/audit-log/export/route.ts:79-88 runs `SELECT ... FROM admin_audit_log al LEFT JOIN users au ... LEFT JOIN users tu ... ORDER BY al.created_at DESC` with no WHERE and no LIMIT, buffers all rows into a JS array (line 81) and then `JSON.stringify(result.rows, null, 2)` (line 104) -- the entire audit table held in the Node heap twice. (c) lib/notifications/posture-digest.ts:80-93 runs `SELECT DISTINCT ON (url) url, findings FROM scan_history WHERE user_id = $1 AND status = 'completed' ORDER BY url, scanned_at DESC` with no LIMIT and no time bound, and it is called twice per user at lines 113-117. (d) app/api/v3/data-request/route.ts:167-174 selects `findings` for every scan the user ever ran.
findings.impact: (b) is the sharpest: an admin clicking Export on a mature instance OOM-kills the single Node process that also runs every in-flight scan, since `admin_audit_log` grows on every staff action and there is no bound at all. (a) and (d) ship tens of megabytes per request for users with many scans. (c) makes the digest worker's cost scale with total history rather than with what the digest actually reports.
findings.recommendation: Add `findings_count` to (a) and drop `findings` from the projection entirely. Stream (b) with a keyset-paged cursor and write CSV/NDJSON incrementally instead of building one string, and bound it with the same retention window lib/database/audit-log-archive.ts:80 uses. Give (c) a `LIMIT` and a `scanned_at > NOW() - INTERVAL '...'` bound, and project only the finding fields the digest renders. Page (d) or stream it to a file.

findings.title: Single requests fan out more concurrent queries than the entire connection pool holds: 25 from the data-export route against a pool max of 10
findings.description: `CONFIG_DB_POOL_MAX` is 10 (lib/config/config-values.ts:393), wired into the Pool at lib/database/db.ts:58. app/api/v3/data-request/route.ts:97-122 destructures 25 results from a single `Promise.all` at line 123, each of them a `pool.query` -- so one request asks for 25 connections at once and queues on itself for 15 of them, several of which are unbounded (sessions at :137-143, api_usage joined to api_keys at :155-164, all of scan_history with findings at :167-174, scan_tags at :178-183). app/api/v3/admin/route.ts:146 fans out exactly 10 in the `user-detail` branch, monopolizing the pool. app/api/v3/dashboard/route.ts:33 fans out 7 (perf-06), and app/api/v3/admin/billing-overview/route.ts:103 fans out 7 including three full `users` counts. Separately, lib/database/cleanup.ts:481-498 fires `2 x N` unawaited `.catch()`ed writes for expired browser sessions with no cap.
findings.impact: Any one of these requests can starve every other request in the process -- including `getSession`, so an admin opening a user detail page can make other users' logins hang until `connectionTimeoutMillis` fires. The pool is a process-wide resource and nothing in the codebase budgets it per request.
findings.recommendation: Cap fan-out per request. Either raise `CONFIG_DB_POOL_MAX` well above the largest fan-out and size Postgres accordingly, or (better) batch: the data-export route's 25 queries are mostly `WHERE user_id = $1` on different tables and can run in chunks of 4-5, and the admin user-detail branch can be consolidated into 2-3 joined queries. Add an explicit concurrency limiter to the cleanup fan-out at lib/database/cleanup.ts:481.

findings.title: checkExposedFiles fires 23 unthrottled parallel requests at the scan target, and checkLiveFetch adds three more branches on top
findings.description: `checkExposedFiles` builds a 23-entry probe list (paths /.git/config, /.git/HEAD, /.env, /.env.local, /.htpasswd, /phpinfo.php, /info.php, /docker-compose.yml, /phpmyadmin/, /adminer.php, /backup.sql, /terraform.tfstate, /wp-json/wp/v2/users, /metrics, /.npmrc, /.env.production, /web.config, /debug.log, /package-lock.json, /jenkins/, /consul/, /minio/, /rabbitmq/) and dispatches all of them at once with `Promise.allSettled(probes.map(async (probe) => ...))` at lib/scanner/async-checks.ts:3500, each with a 5s timeout. Its caller `checkLiveFetch` runs it concurrently with `checkRobotsTxt`, `checkSecurityTxt` and `checkBucketListing` (lines 4399-4404), and `runAsyncChecksDetailed` runs that branch concurrently with the DNS, TLS, reputation and OSV branches. There is no per-target concurrency cap anywhere in the async layer.
findings.impact: Every scan opens 25+ simultaneous connections to the target within a few hundred milliseconds. Rate-limited targets and WAFs respond by 429ing or blocking, which silently turns real findings into non-findings, and it makes VulnRadar look like an attacker to the site it was asked to assess. On a crawl this repeats per page (perf-03), so a 25-page crawl fetches /.git/config 25 times.
findings.recommendation: Add a small concurrency limiter (4-6 in flight) around the probe dispatch at lib/scanner/async-checks.ts:3500 and share one limiter across every branch that talks to the same origin, so the whole scan presents a bounded, polite request rate. Cache the exposed-files result per origin so a crawl probes each path once.

findings.title: The nightly cleanup runs about thirty DELETEs, four of them full table scans, inside one 350-line transaction holding a pooled connection
findings.description: `lib/database/cleanup.ts` opens `BEGIN` at line 114 and does not `COMMIT` until line 464, wrapping roughly thirty DELETE statements across sessions, rate_limits, tokens, scan_history, scan_finding_feedback, user_notifications, github_review_usage, ai_conversations and more in a single transaction on one pooled client. Four of those DELETEs cannot use an index and seq-scan their table (see perf-15): rate_limits (line 211), scan_finding_feedback (line 380), user_notifications (line 389), github_review_usage (line 401). None of the work is transactionally coupled -- these are independent retention prunes on unrelated tables.
findings.impact: One of the 10 pool connections is held for the entire pass, and every row deleted stays locked for its duration, so any concurrent write touching those rows blocks. The four full scans make the pass length grow with total table size rather than with the number of rows actually being deleted. A failure at line 480 rolls back thirty prunes that had nothing to do with each other.
findings.recommendation: Split the pass in lib/database/cleanup.ts:114-464 into one autocommitted statement per table (or small groups), with the batching pattern `DELETE ... WHERE ctid IN (SELECT ctid ... LIMIT 5000)` in a loop for the large tables, so no single statement holds locks for long. Add the four missing indexes from perf-15 first.

findings.title: checkAccessRules runs two uncached sequential-scan queries on every scan, and once per URL on every bulk or crawl request
findings.description: `checkAccessRules` always issues a blacklist query (lib/scanner/access-rules.ts:56-73) and, when that misses, a `SELECT COUNT(*)::int AS count FROM access_rules WHERE rule_type = 'whitelist' AND is_active = true ...` (lines 100-104) -- two sequential round trips, with no caching anywhere. Both predicates are non-sargable: `LOWER($1) = LOWER(value) OR LOWER($1) LIKE '%.' || LOWER(value)` builds the LIKE pattern from the column, and the IP branch casts `value::inet` (line 51), so neither `idx_access_rules_value` (instrumentation.ts:1022) nor `idx_access_rules_type` (:1023) can be used. It is called on every scan (app/api/v3/scan/route.ts:285), once per URL in `checkAccessRulesBatch`'s sequential loop (lib/scanner/access-rules.ts:160-161), and once per crawl page before the crawl starts (lib/scanner/execute-crawl-scan.ts:423-428).
findings.impact: Two extra serialized round trips on the front of every scan, and `2 x N` for a 100-URL bulk request or a 250-page crawl selection -- up to 500 round trips just to check an admin blocklist that changes maybe once a month.
findings.recommendation: Cache the `access_rules` table in process with a short TTL and an explicit invalidation from the admin write path, exactly as lib/config/runtime-config.ts:63 and lib/tags/auto-tags.ts:702 already do for their tables, and evaluate the match in JavaScript. That turns `checkAccessRulesBatch` and the crawl pre-check into zero queries.

findings.title: Nine admin and public list routes pair a full COUNT(*) with the paged SELECT, most of them running the two back to back instead of in parallel
findings.category: unbounded COUNT on every page load
findings.description: `COUNT(*)` in Postgres always scans the full matching set; a LIMIT on the sibling query does not bound it. Confirmed instances, all on growing tables: app/api/v3/admin/route.ts:269-271 counts all of `admin_audit_log`, awaited AFTER the paged select at :257-268 rather than alongside it, and that paged select uses `LIMIT $1 OFFSET $2` (line 266) so deep pages re-scan and discard every preceding row; :329-338 runs ten scalar sub-selects on the default admin dashboard including two full `scan_history` counts and a full `users` count; :344/:359 add a correlated `(SELECT COUNT(*) FROM scan_history sh WHERE sh.user_id = u.id)` per listed user; :371-375 counts `users` behind a leading-wildcard ILIKE; :300-321 runs three `admin_audit_log` counts per staff row in the polled active-admins section. Same sequential COUNT-then-page shape in app/api/v3/admin/error-logs/route.ts:66 (over an unindexable `message ILIKE '%..%'`), app/api/v3/admin/email-logs/route.ts:81, app/api/v3/admin/content/route.ts:56 and :76, app/api/v3/admin/support-tickets/route.ts:61 (a `GROUP BY status` with no WHERE at all), and app/api/v3/public-scans/route.ts:77 (perf-04).
findings.impact: Opening the admin panel triggers several full-table counts, and the audit-log and email-log searches scan their whole table twice per keystroke-driven page load. The public-scans one is unauthenticated. As the instance ages every one of these gets linearly slower with no upper bound.
findings.recommendation: For the admin routes, drop the exact total: use keyset pagination with a `hasMore` flag from `LIMIT n+1`, or an approximate count from `pg_class.reltuples` where a number must be shown. Where a real count is required, at minimum run it inside the same `Promise.all` as the page query instead of sequentially (app/api/v3/ai/conversations/route.ts:167-178 already does this correctly and is the pattern to copy).

findings.title: Worker failure escalation only sees pass-level throws, so a worker where every single item fails resets its streak to zero and never alerts
findings.category: no monitoring on a silent break
findings.description: createFailureEscalator (lib/admin/failure-escalation.ts:67) only fires sendAdminAlert after `threshold` consecutive recordFailure calls, and recordSuccess resets the streak to 0 (:82-87). Two of the five workers using it can never reach the threshold. In lib/scanner/scheduled-scans-worker.ts, processSchedule catches every per-schedule failure at :359-375 and returns `{ outcome: "error" }` rather than rethrowing; runDueSchedules (:413-433) folds those into `errors: results.filter(r => r.outcome === "error").length` and returns normally; the interval at :467-481 then calls `escalator.recordSuccess()` (:475) with no reference to stats.errors at all. lib/notifications/posture-digest.ts has the identical shape: the per-user catch increments `stats.errors++` (:254-255) and the interval calls `escalator.recordSuccess()` (:304) regardless. So a pass in which 100% of due scheduled scans failed, or 100% of digest emails bounced, is recorded as a healthy pass and the streak never gets past 1.
findings.impact: Scheduled scans are a paid-plan feature. If every schedule starts failing (executeScan throwing, the mail relay rejecting, a bad deploy), the alerting mechanism written specifically for that case ("The scheduled-scans worker is failing on every pass -- due scheduled scans are not running", :479) provably never fires. The only trace is one console.error line per schedule per tick in system_error_logs, which is pull-only and drowned by volume: the escalator resets on the very same tick that produced those errors.
findings.recommendation: In lib/scanner/scheduled-scans-worker.ts:469-475, branch on the returned stats: `if (stats.processed > 0 && stats.scanned === 0 && stats.errors > 0) escalator.recordFailure(...)` else `escalator.recordSuccess()`. Apply the same change to lib/notifications/posture-digest.ts:299-304 using `stats.sent === 0 && stats.errors > 0`. Also check lib/domains/reverify-worker.ts:130-137 for the same per-item swallow before relying on its escalator.

findings.title: Raw exception messages from the scan pipeline are persisted into scan_history.error_message and rendered verbatim to the user with a Copy button
findings.description: lib/scanner/execute-scan.ts:1112-1118 takes any non-cancellation throw from the whole scan pipeline and does `const message = error instanceof Error ? error.message : ...; await finalizeScanFailure(scanId, message)`. lib/scanner/execute-crawl-scan.ts:830-833 is identical. app/api/v3/scan/route.ts:430-433 does the same for a dispatch-time throw. finalizeScanFailure (lib/scanner/scan-jobs.ts:364-380) writes that string straight into `scan_history.error_message`. GET /api/v3/scan/status/[id] then returns it unmodified: `responseBody.error = row.error_message ?? "The scan failed."` (app/api/v3/scan/status/[id]/route.ts:219). The dashboard renders it as-is in a monospace block at components/scanner/dashboard-error-state.tsx:257-259, next to a "Copy error details" button (:235) that copies it to the clipboard. Nothing between the throw and the screen sanitizes the string, so a pg driver message (`relation "scan_tags" does not exist`, `connect ECONNREFUSED 10.0.0.5:5432`), a Node DNS error naming an internal host, or an unexpected library stack message reaches the end user and is retained in the scan row. This is the same class AUDIT-011#brow-01 filed for the browser-session viewer, on a much higher-traffic path.
findings.impact: A user hitting an internal server problem sees the server's own infrastructure details (internal hostnames, private IPs, table and column names) presented as their scan result, and the string is persisted in scan_history for the retention period. It also makes the error UI's classifyError (dashboard-error-state.tsx:44-80) misfire, since it substring-matches on words like "invalid" and "private" that appear in driver text for unrelated reasons.
findings.recommendation: In lib/scanner/execute-scan.ts:1113 and lib/scanner/execute-crawl-scan.ts:831, keep the raw message in the existing console.error and pass a mapped, fixed reason to finalizeScanFailure (a small enum: target unreachable / target blocked / scan timed out / internal error, plus the scan id). Same for app/api/v3/scan/route.ts:431. That keeps app/api/v3/scan/status/[id]/route.ts:219 safe without changing its shape.

findings.title: Client-side render crashes are logged only to the visitor's own browser console, while app/error.tsx tells them "This has been logged"
findings.description: Every error boundary in the app reports into the browser only. app/error.tsx:21-23 is `useEffect(() => { console.error(\`[${APP_NAME}] Unhandled error:\`, error); }, [error])`; app/global-error.tsx:19-21, app/dashboard/error.tsx:24-25, app/admin/error.tsx:14-15, app/history/error.tsx:14-15 and app/profile/error.tsx are all the same one-liner. lib/database/error-log-capture.ts's installErrorLogCapture wraps console.error on the server only, from instrumentation.ts's register() (see its file header at :1-17), so none of those calls ever reach system_error_logs. There is no client-error reporting endpoint anywhere under app/api (no route matching error/telemetry/report other than the admin read-only viewers app/api/v3/admin/error-logs and email-logs). Meanwhile app/error.tsx:58-61 renders the sentence "This has been logged. Try again, or come back once we have looked at it." and the error.digest panel at :63-90 only renders when `error.digest` exists, which for a client-only render error it does not.
findings.impact: The operator has zero visibility into client-side breakage. This project's single most-reported production failure mode is stale-deploy chunk 404s served as text/html (see the deploy-chunk-mismatch history), which manifests exactly as a client-side throw, and none of it is recorded server-side. The user is simultaneously told the error was logged, which is false, and given no reference to quote to support.
findings.recommendation: Add a small rate-limited POST /api/v3/client-errors that accepts `{ message, digest, route }`, console.errors it server-side (which routes it into system_error_logs via the existing wrapper), and call it from app/error.tsx:22 and app/global-error.tsx:20 alongside the existing console.error. Change the copy at app/error.tsx:59 to only claim the error was logged when a digest or a successful report exists.

findings.title: Metering and quota-refund side effects are fire-and-forget with a no-op catch, so a persistent failure silently under-bills usage and leaks concurrency slots
findings.description: Five money- or capacity-affecting writes are started and discarded with `.catch(() => {})`, which logs nothing on any path. lib/database/cleanup.ts:490 `recordBrowserbaseSeconds(row.user_id, elapsedSeconds).catch(() => {})` is the true-up for browser sessions that expired without an explicit DELETE, and :497 `releaseConcurrencySlot().catch(() => {})` frees the global slot each of those rows held. lib/scanner/page-screenshot.ts:276 and :279 are the same two calls on the live scan path. app/api/v3/browser/sessions/route.ts:358 is the third releaseConcurrencySlot site. app/api/v3/scan/github/route.ts:195 and :210 do `await releaseFreeGithubReviewTrial(userId).catch(() => {})`, the refund that gives a user back their one daily free GitHub review when the review threw or produced nothing. The swallow is deliberate in each case (a usage write must not fail the cleanup pass or the scan), but the absence of any log means a persistent failure is undetectable. lib/browserbase/concurrency-queue.ts:146-151 makes the slot case concrete: releaseConcurrencySlot decrements `inFlight` and then awaits `getSetting("BROWSERBASE_MAX_CONCURRENT_SESSIONS")` before calling `admit(...)`, so a throw from getSetting leaves the queue's waiters unadmitted with the counter already decremented, and the `.catch(() => {})` hides it.
findings.impact: Browserbase seconds are what the account is metered on. If recordBrowserbaseSeconds starts failing (a constraint change, a dropped column, a connection ceiling), usage stops being counted against every account and the operator's real Browserbase bill diverges from recorded usage with no error visible anywhere. A failing releaseConcurrencySlot leaks the global session slot permanently, so queued browser sessions wait out their timeout and eventually nobody can start one. A failing releaseFreeGithubReviewTrial silently burns a user's one free daily review for a run that returned nothing.
findings.recommendation: Replace `() => {}` with `(err) => console.error("...", err)` at all seven sites: lib/database/cleanup.ts:490 and :497, lib/scanner/page-screenshot.ts:276 and :279, app/api/v3/browser/sessions/route.ts:358, app/api/v3/scan/github/route.ts:195 and :210. The swallowing behaviour is correct and should stay; only the silence needs fixing, and console.error routes these into system_error_logs for free. Separately, move the `inFlight--` in lib/browserbase/concurrency-queue.ts:148 into a try/finally around the getSetting await.

findings.title: No request or scan correlation id exists anywhere, and system_error_logs stores only a free-text message with no level, route, user, or scan column
findings.description: The only structured error store is system_error_logs, created at instrumentation.ts:636-641 as `(id SERIAL, message TEXT, detail TEXT, created_at TIMESTAMPTZ)`. lib/database/error-log-capture.ts:169-173 inserts exactly `(message, detail)`, formed by string-joining whatever arguments a console.error call happened to pass. There is no level column (console.warn is not captured at all, only console.error at :137), no route, no user id, no scan id, and no request id. Nothing in the app generates a request id: no middleware.ts code sets or reads an x-request-id header, and the only `requestId` identifiers in the tree belong to unrelated features (app/api/v3/scan/discover/route.ts:96 for discovery progress, lib/browserbase/network-capture.ts:76 for CDP frames). GET /api/v3/admin/error-logs (app/api/v3/admin/error-logs/route.ts:37) can therefore only offer page/limit/free-text search over message and detail. The gap is visible in the product copy: components/scanner/dashboard-error-state.tsx:129 tells the user "The error is logged with the reference below" and no reference is ever rendered, because DashboardErrorState has no id prop at all (:22-33).
findings.impact: When a user reports "my scan failed around 3pm", an operator cannot filter to that user or that scan. They grep free-form English across every console.error the process made, from 328 call sites, with a coalescing window and a 100-insert-per-minute cap (error-log-capture.ts:73-79) that can drop exactly the burst they are looking for. Any multi-hop failure (route -> executeScan -> a check -> safeFetch) produces several unrelated-looking rows with nothing tying them together.
findings.recommendation: Add `level`, `route`, `user_id`, `scan_id` and `request_id` columns to system_error_logs in instrumentation.ts and populate them from an AsyncLocalStorage context set in middleware.ts (generate a request id there, echo it as x-request-id). Have lib/database/error-log-capture.ts read that context in the wrapper at :137. Thread scanId into the scanner's console.error calls. Then surface the id in components/scanner/dashboard-error-state.tsx so the sentence at :129 is true.

findings.title: A missing STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET is reported as "Invalid signature" and returns 400 to Stripe, with no admin alert distinguishing misconfiguration from an attack
findings.description: getWebhookSecret (app/api/v3/webhooks/stripe/route.ts:105-111) throws `new Error("STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET environment variable is not set")`, but it is only ever called from inside the signature try block at :154: `event = stripe.webhooks.constructEvent(body, signature, getWebhookSecret());`. The catch at :155-158 treats that identically to a forged signature: `console.error("Webhook signature verification failed:", err); return NextResponse.json({ error: "Invalid signature" }, { status: 400 })`. Every real Stripe event then fails the same way. No sendAdminAlert is called on this path, even though lib/admin/alert-webhook.ts exists and instrumentation.ts:3490 and :3530 already use it for exactly this class of "the deployment is misconfigured" event. The route's own configured-check just above (:140-146) covers only a missing Stripe client, not a missing webhook secret.
findings.impact: A deploy that loses STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET breaks every subscription lifecycle event (created, updated, deleted, invoice paid, credit purchase, refund, dispute) for as long as Stripe keeps retrying, and the log line says "signature verification failed", which reads as an attacker probing the endpoint rather than a config error. Nothing pages anyone, so the first symptom is a customer whose paid plan never activated or whose cancellation never applied.
findings.recommendation: Read process.env.STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET before the try at :153, and on absence return 503 with a distinct log line and a `sendAdminAlert({ event: "stripe_webhook_secret_missing", severity: "critical", ... })`. Keep the 400 "Invalid signature" path strictly for a genuine constructEvent signature failure.

findings.title: Signup returns 409 for a registered email and 200 for an unregistered one, handing back the enumeration oracle login and password-reset close
findings.description: app/api/v3/auth/signup/route.ts:147-150 does `const existing = await getUserByEmail(email); if (existing) return ApiResponse.conflict(ERROR_MESSAGES.DUPLICATE_EMAIL);` -- a deterministic 409-vs-200 split on whether an address has an account. The rest of the auth surface works hard to avoid exactly this: login returns one generic 401 for both 'no user' and 'wrong password' and burns a dummy scrypt hash to equalize timing (app/api/v3/auth/login/route.ts:78-86), forgot-password always returns the same 'If an account with that email exists' message (forgot-password/route.ts:64-76), and resend-verification returns the same string on all three outcomes (resend-verification/route.ts:221-236). The route's own comment at lines 124-128 names the problem ('an attacker who rotates IPs via residential proxy can enumerate which emails are registered (409 "already in use" vs 200 success differentiates them)') and answers it with a per-email limit of 5 per hour at line 130 -- which does not remove the oracle at all, because the FIRST request for any address already answers the question. The per-IP `signup:${ip}` bucket is 5 per 15 minutes, so a single residential-proxy pool tests thousands of addresses a day.
findings.impact: Every enumeration defense elsewhere in the auth surface is nullified: an attacker confirms which of a scraped address list has VulnRadar accounts by posting each one to /signup once, then targets those addresses with credential stuffing or phishing that names the product. For a security-tools vendor, the membership list itself ('who at $COMPANY uses a vulnerability scanner') is the interesting output.
findings.recommendation: Make signup answer identically for both cases: on a duplicate email, return the same 200 `SUCCESS_MESSAGES.SIGNUP` + `requiresVerification: true` body the new-account path returns, and instead of creating a row, send the existing account an 'someone tried to sign up with your address, sign in or reset your password' email. Keep the per-email bucket as flood control. The signup form then always shows 'check your email', and the real disambiguation happens in the inbox, which only the address owner can read.

findings.title: Turning 2FA off leaves device_trust rows intact, so a previously trusted device skips the second factor when 2FA is turned back on
findings.description: app/api/v3/auth/2fa/disable/route.ts:56-59 clears `totp_enabled`, `two_factor_method`, `totp_secret`, and `backup_codes`, and app/api/v3/auth/2fa/email-setup/route.ts:332-338 (DELETE) clears the first two plus email_2fa_codes -- neither deletes from device_trust. Rows written by upsertTrustedDevice (lib/auth/device-trust.ts:89-116) live for DEVICE_TRUST_DAYS, default 30 (lib/config/config-values.ts:266), and findTrustedDevice (line 14) only checks `user_id + device_fingerprint + expires_at > NOW()`. So a device trusted on day 1, with 2FA disabled on day 2 and re-enabled on day 3, still satisfies the trusted-device bypass at app/api/v3/auth/login/route.ts:187, app/api/v3/auth/oauth/[provider]/callback/route.ts:369, and app/api/v3/auth/discord/callback/route.ts:278 for the remaining 27 days. The two other places that rotate a credential do get this right and explicitly say why: app/api/v3/auth/reset-password/route.ts:231 and app/api/v3/auth/update/route.ts:348 both `DELETE FROM device_trust WHERE user_id = $1` alongside the session wipe, with a comment about not leaving a planted trust row behind.
findings.impact: A user who turns 2FA off and back on -- the documented way to re-enroll a new authenticator app, since app/api/v3/auth/2fa/setup/route.ts:51-55 refuses to re-enroll while 2FA is active -- believes they have started clean. Any browser that was trusted before, including one an attacker had transient access to, keeps skipping the prompt. The trusted-devices UI (app/api/v3/auth/trusted-devices/route.ts) will list it, but nothing prompts the user to look there during re-enrollment.
findings.recommendation: Add `await pool.query("DELETE FROM device_trust WHERE user_id = $1", [session.userId])` to app/api/v3/auth/2fa/disable/route.ts right after the UPDATE at line 56, and to the DELETE handler in app/api/v3/auth/2fa/email-setup/route.ts after line 332 -- matching what reset-password and the password-change path already do.

findings.title: validateApiKey compares the decrypted key with === and falls through to two unindexed full scans of api_keys on every failed lookup
findings.description: Two issues in the same function. (1) After the O(1) locator lookup, the key itself is checked with a plain `if (decrypted === key)` at lib/api/api-keys.ts:350 and again at :374 -- a short-circuiting comparison on a secret, in a file that otherwise reaches for keyed HMAC and bcrypt. Everywhere else in the auth surface a secret compare uses timingSafeEqual: lib/auth/password-hash.ts:92,117, lib/auth/totp.ts:179, lib/auth/pending-2fa.ts:346, lib/auth/oauth-state.ts:137, lib/auth/ipv4-echo-token.ts:248, app/api/v3/auth/2fa/verify/route.ts:233, and the nonce check at app/api/v3/auth/oauth/[provider]/callback/route.ts:131. (2) When the locator query returns no match -- which is every request carrying a wrong or made-up key -- control falls through to the legacy backfill query at line 366 (`WHERE ak.key_locator IS NULL AND ak.key_encrypted IS NOT NULL`, decrypting each returned row) and then the bcrypt fallback at line 393 (`WHERE ak.key_hash IS NOT NULL AND ak.key_locator IS NULL AND ak.key_encrypted IS NULL`, running bcrypt.compare per row at cost 12). Neither predicate is indexable, so both are sequential scans of api_keys, and both run on every single unauthenticated bad-Bearer request against any of the ~15 Bearer routes.
findings.impact: The timing side of this is largely academic (the locator already narrows the candidate set to one row and the key has 256 bits of entropy), but it is a gratuitous deviation from the rule the rest of this codebase follows. The scan side is concrete: an unauthenticated attacker sending garbage Bearer tokens forces two full table scans of api_keys per request at zero cost to themselves, and if any legacy bcrypt rows exist, one bcrypt-cost-12 verification per row per request -- roughly 250ms of CPU per legacy row, on a route with no rate limit in front of it.
findings.recommendation: Replace both `decrypted === key` comparisons in lib/api/api-keys.ts (lines 350, 374) with a length-checked `timingSafeEqual(Buffer.from(decrypted), Buffer.from(key))`. Guard the two legacy fallbacks so they only run when legacy rows can actually exist: cache a boolean from a one-time `SELECT EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM api_keys WHERE key_locator IS NULL)` at module scope (invalidated on the backfill UPDATE at line 378), and skip lines 366-410 entirely when it is false. Add a partial index `CREATE INDEX ON api_keys (id) WHERE key_locator IS NULL` in instrumentation.ts if the fallback must stay unconditional.

findings.title: Changing the account email leaves every other session and trusted device alive, unlike the password change in the same handler
findings.description: PATCH /api/v3/auth/update treats email and password as the same class of 'sensitive change' at line 68 and gates both behind the same re-auth + `profile-reauth` bucket (lines 70-115). The two branches then diverge. The password branch at lines 337-356 calls deleteAllSessions(), deletes every device_trust row, mints a fresh session, and tells the user 'All other sessions have been signed out for security'. The email branch at lines 207-216 runs `UPDATE users SET email = $1, email_verified_at = NULL` plus sendEmailVerification and stops -- no session wipe, no device_trust wipe. The address the account's password-reset, 2FA email codes, and every security notification are delivered to has just changed identity, and every session that existed a moment earlier is still valid.
findings.impact: An attacker who has a session plus the password (or, for an OAuth-only account, just the session -- lines 116-122 skip the password check entirely there) repoints the account to their own address and keeps every device they were signed in on. The legitimate owner is notified at both addresses (lines 224-247), but if they respond by changing the password they will not think to also check active sessions, and the attacker's own session is not what gets killed. It is also an internal inconsistency: the handler's own comment at lines 201-206 explains that email change is an account-takeover vector, then does not apply the mitigation it applies one branch down.
findings.recommendation: In app/api/v3/auth/update/route.ts, after the email UPDATE at line 207, run the same three statements the password branch runs at lines 343-356: `deleteAllSessions(session.userId)`, `DELETE FROM device_trust WHERE user_id = $1`, then `createSession(...)` and set the refreshed cookie (the code at lines 393-400 can be lifted into a small helper shared by both branches), and return the same `sessionInvalidated: true` flag so the client shows the same message.

findings.title: PUBLIC_PATHS prefix matching silently exempts session-authenticated mutating endpoints from the middleware CSRF check
findings.description: middleware.ts:273-292 returns early for any path matching PUBLIC_PATHS, before the CSRF block at :316. isExemptFromCsrf (:350-368) is documented as "intentionally narrow ... every entry needs a clear non-CSRF trust boundary" and lists six exact paths, but PUBLIC_PATHS creates a second, prefix-matched exemption list that the comment does not account for. Two session-authenticated mutating endpoints land in it: "/api/v3/badge" (public-paths.ts:154) prefix-matches app/api/v3/badge/site/route.ts's POST (:14), PATCH (:64) and DELETE (:95), all of which require getSession() and write host_badges rows; and API_V3.AUTH.ACCEPT_TOS (public-paths.ts:25) covers app/api/v3/auth/accept-tos/route.ts's POST, which does `UPDATE users SET tos_accepted_at = NOW()` for the session user. Two state-changing GETs are also exempt: app/api/v3/stripe/setup-products/route.ts and setup-webhook/route.ts (public-paths.ts:130-131) create live Stripe products/prices and a live Stripe webhook endpoint, and a GET is carried by a SameSite=Lax cookie on a top-level navigation, so a link an admin clicks is enough to fire them.
findings.impact: The CSRF middleware is the app's stated defence for mutating API calls, and these routes silently sit outside it. SameSite=Lax on the session cookie still blocks the cross-site POST cases in current browsers, so this is defence-in-depth rather than a live exploit - but the GET-triggered Stripe setup routes are reachable by a plain link click from an attacker page, and any future same-site-but-different-origin position (a subdomain takeover) collapses the Lax protection for the badge and accept-tos writes too.
findings.recommendation: In middleware.ts, move the `if (pathname.startsWith("/api/v3/") && !isExemptFromCsrf(pathname))` CSRF block above the `if (isPublicPath)` early return at :273 so being publicly reachable no longer implies being CSRF-exempt, and add the genuinely unauthenticated POST endpoints (login, signup, forgot-password, reset-password, 2fa/verify, contact, demo-scan, unsubscribe) to isExemptFromCsrf only if they actually need it - they are same-origin form posts, so most will pass the check unchanged. Separately, convert app/api/v3/stripe/setup-products and setup-webhook from GET to POST since both mutate external state.

findings.title: The two Stripe setup routes hand-roll an exact role === "admin" check, bypassing requireAdmin's 2FA enforcement and locking out super_admin
findings.description: app/api/v3/stripe/setup-products/route.ts:24-36 does getSession() then `if (session.role !== STAFF_ROLES.ADMIN) return 403`, and app/api/v3/stripe/setup-webhook/route.ts:27-38 does getSession() then a raw `SELECT role FROM users` compared against the string literal "admin". Neither goes through lib/auth/authorization.ts's requireAdmin(), so neither runs passesTwoFactorEnforcement (:138): with ENFORCE_STAFF_2FA on, an admin account with totp_enabled false is refused everywhere else in the admin surface but can still call both of these and write to the live Stripe catalog (products.create / prices.create at setup-products:85 and :112) and create a live Stripe webhook endpoint (setup-webhook:85). The exact-string comparison also excludes super_admin, which every other admin route accepts via STAFF_ROLE_HIERARCHY - AUDIT-011#drift-21 noted that half; the 2FA-enforcement half is separate and unfiled.
findings.impact: The one class of account the ENFORCE_STAFF_2FA toggle is meant to neutralise retains write access to the production Stripe catalog and webhook configuration. Low rather than medium because the caller is still a genuine admin and the operations are near-idempotent, but it is the same bypass pattern as authz-06 and it sits on the billing integration.
findings.recommendation: Replace the hand-rolled checks in both files with `const admin = await requireAdmin(); if (!admin) return ApiResponse.forbidden(...)` from lib/auth/authorization.ts. That fixes the 2FA bypass and the super_admin lockout in one change, and removes the duplicate `SELECT role FROM users` in setup-webhook/route.ts:32.

findings.title: Scan screenshots are readable with no authentication at all, and by sequential legacy id, via the middleware's Bearer-token bypass
findings.description: app/api/v3/scan/screenshot/[id]/route.ts:38 sets `authorized = scan.is_public === true` and only falls back to a session + getTeamResourceAccess check when that is false. scan_history.is_public defaults to true (instrumentation.ts:2190), so most rows qualify. The route is not in PUBLIC_PATHS, but middleware.ts:325 lets any request through when `authorization` merely starts with "Bearer " - the string is never validated there, and this route never validates it either (it only calls getSession()). So `curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer x' https://host/api/v3/scan/screenshot/42` reaches the handler with no identity at all. resolveScanRow (lib/history/resolve-scan.ts:59-67) still matches a legacy numeric primary key alongside the opaque public_id, so the id space is `1..N` sequential. Every sibling per-scan route requires an authenticated owner or team-read (history/[id]/route.ts:117-166, history/[id]/report/route.ts:134-144); this one does not.
findings.impact: An anonymous caller can walk ids 1..N and harvest the stored page screenshot of every public scan, and confirm which scan ids exist. The images are of publicly reachable sites so the content is low-sensitivity, but for a security product it is an unauthenticated enumeration of other tenants' scan activity, and it defeats the opaque public_id the rest of the codebase moved to precisely to stop id-walking.
findings.recommendation: In app/api/v3/scan/screenshot/[id]/route.ts, require a session before the is_public shortcut (move the `getSession()` call above :38 and 404 when there is none), so the public surface stays the token-scoped app/api/v3/shared/[token]/screenshot route it already documents at :19-21. If truly anonymous access is wanted, at minimum reject the legacy numeric id here by calling scanNumericId and only accepting a public_id match.

findings.title: matchesPathPattern compiles an admin-set notification path filter to `.*` per `*` and runs it in every visitor's browser, the same backtracking shape as the robots matcher
findings.description: matchesPathPattern (lib/notifications/match-path.ts:12-22) escapes the regex metacharacters in an admin-configured `path_pattern`, replaces each `*` with `.*`, and evaluates `new RegExp(`^${escaped}$`).test(pathname)`. That is the identical construction to lib/scanner/crawl-discovery.ts:268-273 (inj-02) and has the same exponential worst case; the module comment says it is deliberately client-safe and used from both the bell dropdown and the site-wide banner renderer (components/shared/notification-center.tsx, components/shared/site-notifications.tsx), so it executes in every visitor's browser on every route change.
findings.impact: An admin (or anyone who gains an admin session, or a compromised staff account) can set a notification targeting pattern such as `/a*a*a*a*a*a*a*a*b` that hangs the main thread of every signed-in visitor's tab. Bounded because the input is admin-only, and there is no cross-tenant consequence, but it is an unnecessary self-inflicted foot-gun in shipped client code.
findings.recommendation: Replace the regex in lib/notifications/match-path.ts with a linear greedy wildcard walk (split on `*`, then advance through pathname with indexOf, anchoring the first and last segments), or reject patterns containing more than two `*` characters in the admin notification form before they are stored.

findings.title: iframe-sandbox check builds a regex by interpolating a raw URL host, so an IPv6 target's `[::1]:8080` host becomes a character class and the same-origin filter silently inverts
findings.description: The third-party-iframe filter at lib/scanner/checks/headers.ts:1422-1429 does `host = new URL(_url).host` (:1418) and then `!new RegExp(`^https?://${host}`, 'i').test(...)` on each iframe's src. `host` is interpolated with no escaping. For an IPv6 target, `new URL('http://[::1]:8080/x').host` is the literal string `[::1]:8080` (verified in Node), so the compiled regex becomes `^https?://[::1]:8080`, in which `[::1]` is a character class matching a single `:` or `1`. `new RegExp('^https?://' + new URL('http://[::1]:8080/x').host, 'i').test('http://[::1]:8080/x')` returns false (verified).
findings.impact: On a self-hosted or internal target addressed by IPv6 literal, the site's own same-origin iframes are classified as third-party and reported as unsandboxed third-party embeds: a false positive in a security report, from a check whose whole purpose is deciding first-party vs third-party. A host containing an unbalanced bracket would instead throw, and the throw is swallowed by runSyncChecks' catch (lib/scanner/engine.ts:171), silently dropping the check.
findings.recommendation: In lib/scanner/checks/headers.ts, stop building a regex. Parse each iframe src with `new URL(src, _url)` and compare `.host` to the target's `.host` directly; that is both correct for IPv6 and cheaper. If a regex is kept, escape the host with the same `replace(/[.*+?^${}()|[\]\\]/g, '\\$&')` used in lib/scanner/crawl-discovery.ts:269.

findings.title: Two admin log-search endpoints still pass an unescaped ILIKE pattern, unlike the user and team search that were fixed for the same issue
findings.description: app/api/v3/admin/email-logs/route.ts:67-71 does `params.push(`%${search}%`)` then `(recipient ILIKE $n OR subject ILIKE $n)`, and app/api/v3/admin/error-logs/route.ts:61-64 does `WHERE message ILIKE $1 OR detail ILIKE $1` with `[`%${search}%`]`. Neither escapes `%`, `_` or `\` and neither adds `ESCAPE '\'`. The sibling searches were fixed for exactly this: app/api/v3/admin/route.ts:127 (`const searchEscaped = search.replace(/[\\%_]/g, '\\$&')`, with the comment 'Without this, typing "%" returns all users (full table scan)') and app/api/v3/admin/teams/route.ts:37/:58 both use `ESCAPE '\'`. These two were left behind. It is not SQL injection: the value is still a bound parameter.
findings.impact: An admin searching email or error logs for a literal `_` or `%` gets wrong results (every underscore matches any character), and a search of `%` degrades to a full scan of system_error_logs / the email log table, which are the two highest-volume tables in the schema. Bounded to staff users.
findings.recommendation: Apply the same one-line escape used at app/api/v3/admin/route.ts:127 in both files, and add `ESCAPE '\'` to each ILIKE clause, matching app/api/v3/admin/teams/route.ts.

findings.title: The scheduled-scans plan limit is a read-then-insert with no guard, so concurrent POSTs let a user exceed their plan's scheduledScans cap
findings.description: POST /api/v3/schedules counts existing rows with `SELECT COUNT(*)::int as count FROM scheduled_scans WHERE user_id = $1` (app/api/v3/schedules/route.ts:134-137), compares it against planLimits.scheduledScans via withinPlanLimit at :139-147, and then does an unguarded `INSERT INTO scheduled_scans ...` at :167-173. There is no row lock, no unique constraint, and no conditional INSERT ... WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) ...) < limit, so two requests that both read the same count before either inserts both pass the gate. The same shape exists for the team seat cap at app/api/v3/teams/members/route.ts:190-205 (count, then INSERT at :214) and the team-count cap at app/api/v3/teams/route.ts:78-91. Contrast lib/rate-limiting/daily-limits.ts, which closes exactly this race for the scan counter with a single guarded upsert (`ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE ... WHERE rate_limits."count" < $2`, :366-368).
findings.impact: A user (or a script) firing N parallel schedule-create requests lands N schedules where the plan allows one more, permanently over the cap until someone notices -- and each extra schedule then runs forever as an unmetered scan source (see logic-01). Bounded by how many requests overlap the same read, and self-limiting because the cap is re-read on the next single request, so the practical overshoot is small. The same argument applies to the team seat cap, where the overshoot is a paid-seat count.
findings.recommendation: In app/api/v3/schedules/route.ts, replace the count-then-insert with a single data-modifying statement: `INSERT INTO scheduled_scans (...) SELECT $1, $2, ... WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM scheduled_scans WHERE user_id = $1) < $limit RETURNING id`, treating a zero-row result as the over-limit rejection (skip the WHERE entirely when the limit is -1). Apply the same shape to the seat check in app/api/v3/teams/members/route.ts:190 and the team-count check in app/api/v3/teams/route.ts:78.

findings.title: FEATURE_SCHEDULED_SCANS is only enforced when a schedule is created; disabling it leaves every existing schedule running
findings.category: feature flag not re-checked at run time
findings.description: The FEATURE_SCHEDULED_SCANS setting is read in exactly one place on this feature's server side: POST /api/v3/schedules returns 403 'Scheduled scans are disabled on this deployment.' when it is false (app/api/v3/schedules/route.ts:71-76). The worker never consults it. runDueSchedules (lib/scanner/scheduled-scans-worker.ts:413) reads only SCHEDULE_WORKER_CLAIM_LIMIT and SCHEDULE_WORKER_BATCH_CONCURRENCY, then claims and processes every active, due row; schedulePeriodicScheduledScans (:455) is registered unconditionally from instrumentation.ts's startup sequence. Neither claimDueSchedules' WHERE clause (:125, `active = true AND next_run_at <= NOW()`) nor processSchedule's gates (:244 target safety, :261 frequency plan tier) reference the flag.
findings.impact: An operator who turns the feature off in /admin to shed load, or because scheduled scanning is causing a problem with a target, sees new schedules blocked but every pre-existing schedule keeps firing full scans on its normal cadence indefinitely. The kill switch reads as a kill switch in the admin UI and is not one. Bounded by how many schedules already exist, but on a deployment with hourly Elite schedules that is exactly the load the operator was trying to stop.
findings.recommendation: At the top of runDueSchedules in lib/scanner/scheduled-scans-worker.ts (before the claimDueSchedules call at :415), `if (!(await getSetting("FEATURE_SCHEDULED_SCANS"))) return { processed: 0, scanned: 0, blocked: 0, planGated: 0, errors: 0 };` -- getSetting is already imported at :46 and the resolver's 30s cache TTL makes the extra read free. Returning empty stats rather than throwing keeps the failure escalator at :466 quiet.

findings.title: The staff plan floor applied on cancellation hardcodes three of the seven staff roles and omits super_admin, so those accounts drop to 'free' instead of their granted floor
findings.category: duplicated role list drifted from its source of truth
findings.description: Three separate cancellation paths reset the plan with the same hand-written CASE: `plan = CASE WHEN role IN ('admin', 'moderator', 'support') THEN 'pro_supporter' ELSE 'free' END` -- app/api/v3/webhooks/stripe/route.ts:640 (customer.subscription.deleted), app/api/v3/billing/subscription/cancel/route.ts:74 (immediate cancel), and app/api/v3/billing/route.ts:425 (cancel_immediately action). The canonical staff-role list is STAFF_ROLES in lib/rate-limiting/daily-limits.ts:22-30, which contains seven roles: admin, moderator, support, billing, security_analyst, content_manager, ops. The CASE covers three of them and, separately, super_admin -- whose granted floor is elite_supporter, not pro_supporter (lib/billing/staff-plan.ts:49, 62-64) -- is in none of the lists. lib/billing/staff-plan.ts's grantStaffPlan/revokeStaffPlan, which own this policy, are not called from any of the three cancel paths.
findings.impact: A billing/security_analyst/content_manager/ops staffer who cancels a real paid subscription has users.plan written to 'free' rather than the pro_supporter floor their role grants. Their enforced limits are mostly unaffected because getUserPlan (lib/rate-limiting/daily-limits.ts:89) tags any STAFF_ROLES member as 'staff' and every resolver substitutes pro_supporter, so this is mainly a wrong displayed plan. A super_admin is the real case: super_admin is deliberately excluded from STAFF_ROLES (:20-21), so getUserPlan falls through to the literal column and returns 'free' -- that account is genuinely dropped to the Free tier's 25 scans/day and free-tier caps after canceling, until the next process restart, when reconcileStaffPlans (lib/billing/staff-plan.ts:253) sweeps it back to elite_supporter (and only if pre_staff_plan is still NULL).
findings.recommendation: Replace the three inline CASE expressions with a call to the module that owns the policy: after the UPDATE that clears the Stripe columns, call grantStaffPlan(userId, role) from lib/billing/staff-plan.ts (exported already), or at minimum parameterise the CASE against STAFF_ROLES plus super_admin rather than a hardcoded triple -- e.g. `plan = CASE WHEN role = 'super_admin' THEN 'elite_supporter' WHEN role = ANY($n::text[]) THEN 'pro_supporter' ELSE 'free' END` with STAFF_ROLES bound as the array.

findings.title: A lapsing Stripe subscription revokes the premium badge even when an active admin gift still entitles the user to it
findings.category: entitlement revoked without checking the other grant path
findings.description: The premium badge has two independent grant paths. The Stripe path calls grantPremiumBadge/revokePremiumBadge from lib/billing/badges.ts. The gift path awards it directly in app/api/v3/admin/route.ts:1674-1691 (SELECT the 'premium' badge id, INSERT INTO user_badges if absent) when an admin runs gift_subscription. revokePremiumBadge (lib/billing/badges.ts:32-48) is an unconditional `DELETE FROM user_badges WHERE user_id = $1 AND badge_id = $2` -- it never looks at gifted_subscriptions. It is called from customer.subscription.updated whenever the resolved plan is free (app/api/v3/webhooks/stripe/route.ts:583), from customer.subscription.deleted (:649), and from confirmSubscription (app/actions/stripe.ts:335). The symmetric case is handled correctly in the other direction: revoke_gift only removes the badge when the user is on the free plan (app/api/v3/admin/route.ts:1709-1721).
findings.impact: A user who has both an active admin gift and a Stripe subscription that then lapses, is canceled, or expires loses the premium badge even though the gift is still live and still grants them the paid plan. The badge is user-visible on shared scans, public scans and the profile (the badges query in app/api/v3/shared/[token]/route.ts:114-119 reads user_badges directly), so the account silently stops being marked as a supporter while still holding a valid gifted subscription. Nothing re-grants it: the gift path only inserts at gift creation, so the badge stays missing until an admin re-issues the gift.
findings.recommendation: Make revokePremiumBadge in lib/billing/badges.ts conditional on there being no other live entitlement: guard the DELETE with `AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM gifted_subscriptions WHERE user_id = $1 AND revoked_at IS NULL AND expires_at > NOW())`, which mirrors the check revoke_gift already makes in the opposite direction at app/api/v3/admin/route.ts:1709. That keeps all three Stripe callers (webhooks :583, :649 and app/actions/stripe.ts:335) correct without changing any of them.

findings.title: The anonymous demo scan abandons runAsyncChecks after its 15 s race, leaving the work and an uncleared timer running with no accounting
findings.description: app/api/v3/demo-scan/route.ts:215-219 builds `const asyncPromise = runAsyncChecks(url)` and races it against `new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(() => resolve([]), asyncChecksTimeoutMs))` (SCAN_ASYNC_CHECKS_TIMEOUT_MS default 15000, lib/config/config-values.ts:566). When the timeout wins, the handler returns but asyncPromise keeps executing -- runAsyncChecks fans out the full live-fetch battery (~23 exposed-file probes per lib/scanner/async-checks.ts:2724, plus GraphQL, bucket-listing and header probes) against the anonymous caller's chosen target with nothing left holding a reference to it. The timeoutPromise's setTimeout is never cleared, so the timer survives to its full 15 s even when the checks finish first. Contrast lib/scanner/execute-scan.ts:573-647, which keeps `asyncTimeoutHandle` and clears it in a finally.
findings.impact: The one endpoint reachable with no account at all can leave outbound probe batteries running past the response, so the visible per-IP demo budget (5 per 12 hours) understates the real outbound volume, and slow targets accumulate detached work in the shared process. Bounded in practice by the per-fetch AbortSignal timeouts inside the checks, which is why this is low rather than higher.
findings.recommendation: In app/api/v3/demo-scan/route.ts, hold the timeout handle and clearTimeout it after the race (as lib/scanner/execute-scan.ts:647 does), and pass an AbortSignal into runAsyncChecks that is aborted when the timeout wins so the abandoned branch actually stops issuing requests.

findings.title: GET /api/v3/host/[hostname] and the badge endpoints are unauthenticated with no rate limiter, so the public-scan corpus can be scraped for free
findings.description: app/api/v3/host/[hostname]/route.ts has no getSession call and no checkRateLimit import; its GET at :70 runs two Postgres queries per request -- a host_reputation lookup at :88-103 and, when source_scan_id is set, a scan_history lookup at :140 -- and returns the full findings JSONB plus result_meta. app/api/v3/host/[hostname]/trend/route.ts, app/api/v3/badge/[token]/route.ts and app/api/v3/whoami-ip/route.ts are in the same position (no session, no limiter), while the sibling public listing endpoint app/api/v3/public-scans/route.ts:48-51 does gate on `public-scans:${ip}` and documents per-IP as "the only throttle available" for exactly this shape of route.
findings.impact: An anonymous caller can enumerate hostnames at line rate and pull the complete finding set for every publicly-listed scan, and each request costs two DB round trips plus a JSONB serialisation from a connection pool shared with the scan workers. It is free compute and free bulk export of the product's differentiating dataset, with no per-IP ceiling to make it slow. Low rather than higher because the data is public by design and both queries are indexed point lookups.
findings.recommendation: Apply the same `checkRateLimit({ key: \`public-scans:${ip}\`, ...RATE_LIMITS.publicScans })` gate used in app/api/v3/public-scans/route.ts:48 to app/api/v3/host/[hostname]/route.ts, its /trend sibling and app/api/v3/badge/[token]/route.ts (use the /64-masked key from abuse-08 so it is not trivially rotated).

findings.title: Three IPv6 range regexes match a single 16-bit group where the comment claims a /7 or /10, leaving fe81::-febf:: and fc00::-fcff:: unblocked
findings.description:
PRIVATE_IPV6_PATTERNS is tested against the canonical 8-group form produced by toCanonicalIPv6 (lib/scanner/safe-fetch.ts:182-232), so each `/^xxxx:/` anchors on the full first group, not a prefix:
- lib/scanner/safe-fetch.ts:80 `/^fe80:/i` is commented "IPv6 link-local (fe80::/10)". fe80::/10 spans first groups fe80 through febf. `fe81::1` canonicalises to `fe81:0000:...` and matches nothing in the list, so isPrivateIP returns false for it.
- lib/scanner/safe-fetch.ts:81 `/^fc00:/i` is commented "fc00::/7". That /7 spans fc00 through fdff. The fd00::/8 half is covered by the separate `/^fd[0-9a-f]{2}:/i` on line 82, but fc01 through fcff match nothing.
- lib/scanner/safe-fetch.ts:98 `/^fec0:/i` is commented "site-local", which is fec0::/10 (fec0-feff); fec1 upward is unmatched.
The same shape is fine for the loopback and unspecified patterns (:79, :83) because those are single addresses, and for the IPv4-mapped patterns (:84-93) because they anchor on the embedded v4 octets.
findings.impact: Bounded in practice: real link-local traffic uses fe80::/64, fc00::/8 was never allocated by IANA, and fec0::/10 is deprecated. But a host that has been configured with an address in fe81::/16-febf::/16 or fc01::/16-fcff::/16 (which is legal, and which some Kubernetes and overlay-network setups do use for ULA space) is reachable through validateScanTarget with no other control in the way. It is also a latent trap: the comments assert coverage the code does not have, so a reviewer confirming "fc00::/7 is blocked" reads the comment and moves on.
findings.recommendation: In lib/scanner/safe-fetch.ts, replace lines 80, 81 and 98 with patterns that match the real prefix lengths: `/^fe[89ab][0-9a-f]:/i` for fe80::/10, `/^f[cd][0-9a-f]{2}:/i` for fc00::/7 (which then subsumes line 82), and `/^fe[c-f][0-9a-f]:/i` for fec0::/10. Or, preferably, fold this into the numeric-CIDR rewrite recommended in ssrf-03 so IPv6 ranges are expressed as prefixes rather than as regexes over a canonicalised string. Add table-driven cases to the `isPrivateIP IPv6 canonicalization` block in tests/lib/scanner/safe-fetch.test.ts:21 for fe81::1, fcff::1 and fec1::1.

findings.title: The BrowserBase screenshot and live-session paths validate only the entry URL; the headless browser's own redirects and sub-resource loads are never checked
findings.category: guard does not cover browser navigations
findings.description:
captureScreenshot calls validateScanTarget(targetUrl) at lib/scanner/page-screenshot.ts:199-203 and then sends `Page.navigate {url: targetUrl}` over CDP at :135. Everything the browser does after that is outside the Node fetch guard: a 302 the page returns, a meta refresh, a `window.location` assignment, and every image/script/XHR/iframe the page pulls. lib/scanner/auth/browser-login.ts has the same shape: validateScanTarget at :375, then `Page.navigate` at :280. The interactive path is the same: app/api/v3/browser/sessions/route.ts:99-108 validates the optional seed `url` once, and the user then drives the session freely from app/browser/[id]/page.tsx. safeFetch's per-hop re-validation (lib/scanner/safe-fetch.ts:654-798) simply does not apply to any of it.

The mitigating fact, which is why this is low and not high: lib/browserbase/client.ts hardcodes BROWSERBASE_BASE_URL to https://api.browserbase.com/v1 (:43) and connects to the session over the returned `connectUrl` (:230-257). There is no local-Chrome or self-hosted-CDP fallback anywhere in lib/browserbase/, so the browser always runs in BrowserBase's cloud. The internal network a redirect could reach is BrowserBase's, not VulnRadar's, and 169.254.169.254 inside that session is BrowserBase's metadata service.
findings.impact: VulnRadar can be pointed, by any user with a plan that allows screenshots or live sessions, at a page that redirects into BrowserBase's internal network or metadata endpoint. That is a third party's blast radius rather than VulnRadar's, but VulnRadar is the vehicle, and the same code becomes a first-party SSRF the moment anyone adds a local-Chrome or self-hosted CDP option for self-hosters (which is the obvious next step for a self-hostable product that today silently disables screenshots without BrowserBase credentials).
findings.recommendation: Enable CDP request interception on the session before the first navigate: `Network.enable` plus `Fetch.enable` with a `Fetch.requestPaused` handler that runs the same isPrivateHostname/validateScanTarget check on every intercepted request URL and calls `Fetch.failRequest` when it fails. Wire it in one place, lib/browserbase/client.ts's openCdpPageSession, so page-screenshot.ts, browser-login.ts and the interactive session route all inherit it. At minimum, subscribe to `Page.frameNavigated` and abort the session when the frame URL leaves the validated host.

findings.title: Neither validateScanTarget nor safeFetch's redirect loop checks the URL scheme, so only the cross-host rule stands between a Location header and a non-HTTP outbound request
findings.description:
The scheme allowlist lives only in assertSafePublicHttpUrl (lib/scanner/safe-fetch.ts:501-534), which safeFetch runs exactly once, on the initial URL (:562). validateScanTarget (:430-494) has no protocol check at all: it parses the URL, looks at the hostname, and returns safe/unsafe. The redirect loop then re-validates each hop with validateScanTarget alone (:746) and never re-runs assertSafePublicHttpUrl, so the next hop's scheme is unexamined. A `Location: ftp://<same-host>/x` or `Location: gopher://<same-host>:70/` passes the sameRegisteredHost test at :730-740 (identical hostname) and the validateScanTarget test at :746-752, and reaches `fetch()` at :686. It fails today only because undici refuses schemes it does not implement. file:, data:, blob: and javascript: are separately blocked, but by accident: their parsed hostname is the empty string, which never equals the initial hostname, so the cross-host branch at :736 throws first.

The same gap is why validateScanTarget is unsafe to use as a standalone guard, and it is used that way in several places: lib/scanner/page-screenshot.ts:199, lib/scanner/checks/tls.ts:247 and :359, lib/scanner/async-checks.ts:2251. Those happen to be fed http(s) URLs by their callers, and validateScanTarget does fail closed on `file:///etc/passwd` (empty hostname to `lookup("")`, which resolves to an empty address list and hits the "resolved to no addresses" refusal at :474-479), but that is a coincidence of Node's dns.lookup behaviour, not a check.
findings.impact: No exploit today: undici rejects ftp/gopher/dict, and the schemes that would matter most (file:, data:, javascript:) are stopped by an unrelated hostname comparison rather than by a scheme check. The consequence is that the scheme allowlist is load-bearing in exactly one place and absent from the two functions that every other module treats as the guard, so a future change to the cross-host rule (for example allowing a redirect to any subdomain of the registered domain, which the walmart.com www-apex work already gestures at) silently re-opens non-HTTP outbound requests, and any new caller of validateScanTarget inherits a guard that does not check what it looks like it checks.
findings.recommendation: Two one-line changes in lib/scanner/safe-fetch.ts. First, add the scheme check to validateScanTarget itself, right after `const parsed = new URL(url)` at :435: `if (!ALLOWED_PROTOCOLS.has(parsed.protocol)) return { safe: false, reason: "Only http and https URLs can be scanned." }`, which hardens every standalone caller at once. Second, in the redirect loop call `assertSafePublicHttpUrl(nextUrlObj.href)` inside a try/catch before the validateScanTarget call at :746 so each hop passes the same syntactic gate the entry URL did. Add a test to tests/lib/scanner/safe-fetch.test.ts asserting a `Location: ftp://example.com/` hop is refused.

findings.title: Four third-party subdomain-discovery APIs are fetched with follow-redirects and unbounded JSON/text reads, outside every SSRF and size guard
findings.description:
fetchCrtSh (lib/scanner/subdomain-discovery-engine.ts:437-450), fetchHackerTarget (:472-486), fetchSubdomainCenter (:500-512) and fetchRapidDns (:522-534), plus the remaining sources at :556, :593, :629, :667 and :705, all call the global `fetch` directly. The host is a hardcoded constant in each case and the user-supplied domain goes through encodeURIComponent, so there is no URL-injection hole. What is missing is everything else safeFetch provides: `redirect` is left at fetch's default of "follow", so any 3xx these endpoints return is followed blindly with no per-hop private-IP re-validation, and the responses are consumed with bare `await res.json()` (:448, :510) and `await res.text()` (:484) with no byte cap. `AbortSignal.timeout(10000-15000)` is passed straight to fetch here (not through safeFetch), so unlike ssrf-01 the time bound does hold, but the size bound does not.

These are free, unauthenticated, third-party endpoints (crt.sh, api.hackertarget.com, api.subdomain.center, rapiddns.io) that VulnRadar has no control over, called on behalf of a user-supplied domain.
findings.impact: A 10-second window at any reasonable bandwidth is hundreds of megabytes buffered into a string per source, and up to nine sources run per discovery. More structurally: if any of these free services is hijacked, expires, or is DNS-poisoned, a `302 Location: http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/` is followed with no guard at all, and the response is parsed and mined for hostnames, turning a third-party outage into a metadata read on VulnRadar's own host.
findings.recommendation: Route all nine calls in lib/scanner/subdomain-discovery-engine.ts through safeFetch, the same way the subdomain HTTP probes at :854 and :865 in the same file already are, and pass `allowedHostnames: ["crt.sh"]` etc. so each source is pinned to its own host and a redirect off it is refused. Cap each read with the shared bounded reader recommended in ssrf-01 rather than `await res.json()` / `await res.text()`.

findings.title: The safe-fetch test suite covers redirects and IPv6 canonicalization but never exercises the address-range gaps, the allowedHostnames argument, or any body bound
findings.category: test gap in the SSRF guard
findings.description:
tests/lib/scanner/safe-fetch.test.ts is 231 lines and 18 cases. It mocks dns/promises (:6-9) and stubs global fetch (:127-131), and it does cover the things prior audits broke: IPv6 canonicalization of ::1 / ::ffff:127.0.0.1 / 64:ff9b:: forms (:21-79), resolve-to-private (:83), the metadata IP (:91), fail-closed on empty DNS (:104) and on DNS error (:204), the redirect-to-metadata and redirect-to-RFC1918 refusals (:141, :156), cross-host redirect refusal (:169), same-host rebind refusal (:184), and the non-http scheme refusal (:227). So the memory note that safeFetch had ZERO tests is stale.

What is not covered maps one-to-one onto the defects filed above:
- No case asserts any bound on the response body, in bytes or in time: the behaviour in ssrf-01 would pass the suite unchanged.
- No case for the `allowedHostnames` parameter (lib/scanner/safe-fetch.ts:574-582), even though it is the stated containment for every active probe (lib/scanner/active-probes/shared.ts:14-19) and it is enforced only on the first hop, not on the www-apex redirect the loop permits.
- No case for the `session` parameter's credential-drop-on-redirect behaviour (lib/scanner/safe-fetch.ts:671-680), the whole reason authenticated scanning is safe.
- No case for 100.64/10, 198.18/15 or 192.0.0.0/24 (ssrf-03), nor for the fe80::/10 and fc00::/7 prefix widths (ssrf-05).
- No case for pinToResolvedIp (lib/scanner/safe-fetch.ts:273) or for the fact that the HTTPS branch does not pin (ssrf-02).
- No case for a hostname in decimal/octal/hex form, which currently relies entirely on getaddrinfo normalising before isPrivateIP runs.
findings.impact: The guard is the single most consequential piece of code in the product, and the parts of it that are currently wrong are exactly the parts with no test. Any of the fixes recommended in ssrf-01 through ssrf-05 can be shipped, then silently regressed, with a green suite.
findings.recommendation: Extend tests/lib/scanner/safe-fetch.test.ts with: a case that stubs fetch with a Response over a never-ending ReadableStream and asserts safeFetch's consumer stops at the byte cap and within the deadline; a case asserting safeFetch rejects a hostname absent from allowedHostnames, and one asserting the www-apex redirect hop is re-checked against that list; a case asserting session headers are attached on-origin and absent after a redirect; table cases for 100.100.100.200, 198.18.0.1, 192.0.0.1, fe81::1, fcff::1 in the existing isPrivateIP block at :21; and a case asserting the fetch dispatcher connects to the validated IP for an https target once ssrf-02 is fixed.

findings.title: jspdf and jspdf-autotable are production dependencies with zero imports, and vitest plus @vitest/coverage-v8 are in dependencies rather than devDependencies
findings.description: package.json:92-93 declares jspdf 4.2.1 and jspdf-autotable 5.0.8 as runtime dependencies. A repo-wide grep for jspdf/jsPDF across every .ts, .tsx and .mjs outside node_modules, .next and the stale worktree returns exactly one hit, and it is a comment: tests/lib/reports/pdf-report.test.ts:8 ('browser-rendering dependency here despite jspdf being in package.json for'). Nothing imports either package. Separately, @vitest/coverage-v8 4.1.11 (package.json:81) and vitest 4.1.11 (package.json:117) are listed under `dependencies` rather than devDependencies, so `npm ci --omit=dev` in a Docker build installs the whole test runner and its v8 coverage toolchain into the production image.
findings.impact: Three unnecessary packages are installed, audited and shipped in every production install and Docker image. The two jspdf packages are also a live supply-chain surface for code that does not exist, and their presence implies a PDF export path that a reader of package.json would go looking for.
findings.recommendation: Remove jspdf and jspdf-autotable from package.json dependencies (and update the comment at tests/lib/reports/pdf-report.test.ts:8), and move vitest and @vitest/coverage-v8 from dependencies to devDependencies. Regenerate package-lock.json on Linux or graft the entries, per the lockfile-platform constraint this repo already documents.

findings.title: The packaged browser extension zips ~606 KB of source maps, and the newly added Chrome Web Store screenshots in extension/public/store will be copied into the next build
findings.description: extension/vite.config.ts:47 sets `sourcemap: true` and extension/scripts/build.mjs:73 sets it again for the background/content bundles. extension/scripts/build.mjs:97 then does `cp(viteOut, dist, { recursive: true })`, and extension/scripts/package.mjs:53 zips the directory with `archive.directory(dist, false)` -- no filter. The current extension/dist-chrome accordingly contains 606 KB of .map files (background.js.map 178 KB, content.js.map 151 KB, popup.js.map 80 KB, constants chunk map 74 KB, options.js.map 64 KB, plans chunk map 50 KB, welcome.js.map 8 KB) against 192 KB of actual shipped code, and both vulnradar-chrome-v0.1.8.zip and vulnradar-firefox-v0.1.8.zip are 232 KB. Separately, extension/vite.config.ts:25 sets `publicDir: extension/public`, so everything under it is copied into the build output; extension/public/store/ was just added and holds five PNGs totalling 516 KB (store_1.png 119,755 bytes through store_5.png 72,067 bytes) that exist only for the Chrome Web Store listing. dist-chrome predates that addition, so the next `npm run build` will copy them into both dist folders and both zips.
findings.impact: Users installing the extension download and store roughly three times the bytes the extension actually runs, and the next release will add another half megabyte of store-listing screenshots that the extension never references. Shipped source maps also hand a reviewer or a repackager the unminified source, which is not a secret in a GPL project but is not intentional either.
